speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, I rise to a double question of privilege, the first one in English and the other in French. In the Ottawa Citizen of July 17 the daily columnist wrote thus:
The development of the day indicated that the terrible-tempered Jean-Fran?ois Pouliot is on the rampage.
I do not object to this, sir; it is a matter of opinion. Then he goes on, making three factual errors in two lines:
Mr. Pouliot opposed the government candidate in Saguenay last winter. . . .
The first factual error is that I opposed no one of the candidates who ran in that county last fall. I opposed no one; I supported one. Then he states that I opposed the government candidate. There was no government candidate there; the government did not give its support to any one of the four candidates in that election. Finally, he mentions Saguenay as the name of the county, when the name is Charlevoix-Saguenay. Then he goes on and says that I aided Mr. Dorion, who was elected as an independent. That is true, and he proved to be one. Then he goes on:
Now, it seems, he is out with a new candidate from Stanstead.
Here is the point I object to, a little further on:
This Stanstead election will be very much of a group affair. There is a racial aspect to it as well.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the independent candidate who has been chosen by the people of Stanstead were running on a racial issue I would surely not support him, and my record in the house proves very well that I have never indulged in any religious or racial controversies of any kind-either in the house or outside of the house.
Now I turn to French. In Le Devoir of Monday last, July 19, I see a report of what has been said by someone.
(Translation):	Mr. Speaker, the Monday
issue of Le Devoir contains a summary of a speech delivered by one Philippe Girard, whom I neither know nor wish to know. The summary of that part of his speech which refers to me is as follows:
Mr. Pouliot has done very good work in Ottawa;-

That is not what prompts me to rise to a question of privilege.
-now, he has been ordered by his leader-
No order has ever been given to me by any one. I have been glad to oblige my colleagues whenever the opportunity to do so arose. Whoever claims that I have received an order from any one in connection with the Stanstead election is uttering a falsehood.
In the second place:
-to go to Stanstead in order to divide the Canadians-
That is another falsehood. I have never sought to divide the Canadians. I have always advocated harmony between French and English speaking Canadians, between the Canadians who are Protestant and those who are Catholic and even those of the Jewish faith.
A third falsehood is this:
-and he has selected as independent candidate Mr. Martin, who, four days previously, had told Mr. Choquette that on no account was anything to be done to divide the French Canadians.
It is odious for a man to utter such falsehoods in public. It is not true at all that I have selected Mr. Martin. I have never selected any one. I have no more selected Mr. Martin as independent candidate in Stanstead than I have selected Mr. Dorion as independent candidate in Charlevoix-Saguenay, but. for one thing, I am sure that Mr. Martin, like Mr. Dorion, will be elected in Stanstead against any opponent.

speechtext: Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 137, to repeal the Japanese Treaty Act, 1913.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will the minister explain?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	A treaty of commerce and navigation was signed between the United Kingdom and Japan on April 3, 1911, and it was adhered to by Canada. The Japanese Treaty Act, 1913, was adopted in that year, declaring the treaty to have the force of law in Canada. A notice, in accordance with the terms of the treaty, to put an end to it was given on July 26, 1941, and according to the terms of the treaty this notice would have become effective on July 26, 1942. In the meantime war was declared between Japan and Canada, and according to the principles of international law the effect of the treaty came to an end with the declaration of war. But the statute is still .on the books, and this is a one-line bill to repeal the statute which gave force of law to that treaty in Canada in 1913.

Japanese Treaty Act

Have similar trade treaties with Italy, Germany and other axis powers been repealed?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is not to my knowledge that there is any legislation giving the effect of law to treaties with Germany and Italy.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: CARTIER BY-ELECTION-ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES- STATEMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement in connection with the matter raised yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well), and which was discussed in this house.
There has not been time thus far to make a sufficiently lengthy inquiry to determine the accuracy of the various affidavits referred to by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and into the material he adduced to support his statement relating to the enumeration carried on in the constituency of Cartier-Montreal. The government has felt, however, that it has a duty to take immediately such 
steps as should serve to remove all doubt and allay all suspicion as to the fair and honest conduct of the election to be held on August 9. It is essential that such steps be taken without delay.
The present returning officer of the constituency was appointed on September 29, 1938. He consequently acted in the election of that year in which the late Mr. Bercovitch was returned as a member of this house. It is true that Mr. Bercovitch ultimately received an acclamation but of course that could not be safely anticipated, and the result was that the returning officer was required to perform practically all the duties requisite to the holding of an election, just as much as if an election had actually been held. The same returning officer acted in the election in 1940, and also in connection with the vote taken on the plebiscite. The chief electoral officer advises me that no complaint whatever was received as to the manner in which he carried on his duties on any of the three occasions.
However, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar indicates that in this election the present Liberal candidate is the uncle of the returning officer. To avoid any suspicion, however unwarranted, that this might give rise to, the chief electoral officer suggested that the assistant chief electoral officer, Mr. Donald Stewart, be appointed at once as supervisory officer and perform the necessary supervisory duties in the constituency until after the election has taken place. The government immediately accepted the suggestion, and Mr. Stewart will assume, in the name of the chief electoral officer the administrative control of the by-election.
The chief electoral officer has also recommended that it would be inadvisable to have a completely new enumeration. There are two principal reasons for this: In the first place it would inevitably delay the election beyond the time fixed for the return to the writ. But a much more serious objection is that enumerators' cards are delivered to each voter at the time the enumeration is made. These cards in most instances are taken by the elector to the polling booth for presentation to the deputy returning officer. It would consequently, in order to avoid confusion, be necessary in the event of a new enumeration to endeavour to collect in all the cards which are presently issued. This would be a very lengthy and in many cases an impossible task; but, unless it were done, it would result in a wide measure of confusion.
The material tabled by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar refers to only a limited number of subdivisions-approximately ten out of a total of 169 in the riding. He stated

Dominion Elections
that this was the result of a very limited check. The government has felt, however, that in view of the conditions disclosed and the allegations made a thorough and complete examination of the whole riding should be made immediately.
In order to effect this and allay any possible suspicion, the chief electoral officer has recommended the appointment of supervising enumerators who will make a thorough house to house check up of the enumeration in each polling division. These supervision enumerators would consist of two for each division.
All members are aware that under the provisions of the Elections Act the returning officer shall give notice to the candidate who at the last preceding election in the electoral district received the highest number of votes and also to the candidate representing at that election a different and opposed political interest who received the next highest number of votes. Unfortunately that rule cannot be applied in this riding as the candidate receiving the second largest number of votes is now serving in the forces overseas and he did not represent any cohesive body of political opinion. The action which it is proposed to take in the emergent condition that now exists should not be deemed to be any precedent that could be cited as in any way abrogating the general rule hereafter unless, of course, where the circumstances are identical with the emergent situation presented in this instance.
The fairest and most advantageous method would, however, under the existing circumstances, appear to be that one of the enumerators should be nominated by the government candidate, and those representing the opposed political interests should nominate one and, as there are two opposition candidates, each should nominate one-half of the opposition enumerators.
Each supervising enumerator will be sworn to the faithful performance of his or her duties on the special form prescribed by the chief electoral officer. They will commence their duties on Thursday morning, July 22, and complete them by Saturday night, the 24th instant.
Whenever such supervising enumerators discover that unqualified or fictitious persons have been included on the enumerators' preliminary list which has been printed and distributed, it will be their duty to prepare an affidavit in form 13 of the Dominion Elections Act and swear such affidavit before the appropriate revising officer. The affidavit attacking the qualifications of the elector in question shall be dealt with by such revising officer during his regular sittings for revision which are scheduled to be held on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday next at places
already advertised by the returning officer Whenever in the case of the house to house check-up it is discovered by the supervising enumerators that a name of a duly qualified elector has been omitted from the list, it shall be their duty to prepare and subscribe to a sworn application in the form No. 15 of the Dominion Elections Act on behalf of such elector and deliver the same to the assistant chief electoral officer who in turn will present it to the appropriate revising officer.
In the event of any disagreement between the supervising enumerators with regard to inclusion of a name on the list of electors, it is to be reported to the assistant chief electoral officer who shall decide the matter.
Arrangements have already been made for the appointment of additional revising officers for each revisal district by the ex officio revising officer and such additional revising officers will sit in the revisal offices already set up by the returning officer.
The chief electoral officer advises that if the above mentioned steps are taken forthwith, in his opinion any and all inaccuracies on the enumerators' preliminary list can be dealt with by the revising officers as prescribed in the elections act and the finally revised list for each polling division, when reprinted, should accurately set out the names of the electors who are duly qualified to vote at the pending by-election.
Time has not allowed the necessary investigation into the culpability of the enumerators who prepared the lists which were referred to by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It is, of course, possible that in some instances the fact that they receive seven cents for each name enumerated proved too much of a temptation to be resisted. But while this may afford an explanation it does not in the least provide any justification.
The 'house can be assured that the investigation will be thorough and complete .and that the penalty clauses in the elections act will be applied. Four enumerators have been discharged and payment of their remuneration withheld. Pitiably small, you will say-and .it is. But in fairness to the returning officer it must be stated that under the act this is t'he limit of his jurisdiction.
However by subsection 18 of section 17 of the elections act it is provided that.
. . . "any enumerator who, wilfully and without reasonable excuse, includes in any list of electors prepared by him the name of any person whose name he has not good reason to believe should be included, or omits to include in such list the name of any person whom he has good reason to believe has the right to have his name included, shall be guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction as in this act provided."
Dominion Elections

This section must be and will be applied by the appropriate officers of the law against any whom investigation reveals are guilty of its breach.
Confidence in the honest and correct functioning of electoral machinery is fundamental in a democracy both in peace and war.
The steps which I have just outlined should remove any doubt and allay any suspicion from the minds of those who wish to see the elections in this country conducted fairly and honourably. Every step is being taken by the government to ensure that this result is attained.

I believe at that time his leader took a definite and final stand against the necessity of doing so. It seems to me that while we are taking all these steps to meet an emergent condition, we should not try to make any new law. If a provision such as that is to be inserted in the Dominion Elections Act, then it should be nation-wide, and not limited to one particular constituency.

subsubtopic: HOME DEFENCE PERSONNEL-AGRICULTURAL LEAVE-PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I gave notice to the

Canadian Army
Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence that I intended to ask a question to-day in connection with the indicated shortage of farm man-power for harvest purposes. Having regard to the many thousands, of men whose services could be utilized for farm purposes during the harvest season, these men being in the home defence army, what changes, if any, are contemplated in connection w'ith the procedure whereby service men may secure leave? To-day the procedure is so involved as to render very difficult the possibility of men, who could render a real service on the farm during the harvest season, securing leave. I believe agriculture generally would like to have a statement so that the position may be clarified.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: HOME DEFENCE PERSONNEL-AGRICULTURAL LEAVE-PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had notice of what my hon. friend asked yesterday, and I am going to give the house a brief outline of what has been done. I want to correct the expression which has been used so frequently in this house and elsewhere. My hon. friend speaks of the men in the home defence army. There is no such thing in Canada as a home defence army. There is the active army in Canada which has in it a certain number of personnel who have been called up for service in Canada and the territorial waters thereof, but there is no such body of men which could be taken and posted to home agricultural work. The active army includes general service men as well as the home defence men, so called. They are all intermingled in the different units. These home defence personnel are part of the active army in Canada and are to-day serving on the coast defences, on the searchlights, on the anti-aircraft guns all over this country. I indicated in my speech to the house that there were in numbers about a division on anti-aircraft work alone. So-called home defence personnel are in the establishments in Newfoundland, in the Bahamas, in the West Indies, in South America-that is to say in British Guiana-in Alaska and in Labrador. My hon. friend talks about a home defence army which might be turned over to agricultural avocations. As I have said, there is no army made up of these, so-called home defence personnel. They are all mixed up together in the different units. To pull these men out would mean completely breaking down of units which are now engaged on duties which the chiefs of staffs, in collaboration with the chiefs of staffs in the United States, have indicated are necessary in order that we may be prepared for what eventualities may arise.
The question of the size of the army is always a matter for consideration and is always under review, but let no one think that somewhere there are men who are just simply walking around doing nothing. The home defence personnel are either on operational duties in Canada, both on the east and west coast-there is one group of men located at vulnerable points in central Canada -or are part of the home war establishment which is servicing the army in Canada and also servicing those men who are training in the training centres as reinforcements for overseas. That is a little different picture from what is perhaps in the public mind. I expressly pointed out the other day that in the training centres, not as home defence establishment but for reinforcements overseas, there are something like fifty or sixty thousand general service personnel. The members of this home defence personnel are needed to replace general service men in the various operational units in order that these general service men may either be retrained for some particular arm of the service for which overseas reinforcements will be required so that they may be sent directly overseas if they are already trained in a suitable arm.
When I spoke on the war appropriation I indicated that the army programme requires that the general service men who are here be made available for overseas. As I told the house when speaking on the defence estimates, one of the purposes of calling men up at the present time is so that they may release the general service men from their duties in Canada. I want to make that clear; I want to emphasize it if I can, because there does seem to be an impression throughout the country that somehow or other there are home defence men who are just standing around not serving any useful purpose. I say that they are serving one of the purposes for which they are particularly required. They are taking the place of men who are going overseas and they are necessary so long as the defence requirements of Canada are to be maintained, as at present advised.
I sympathize with my hon. friend when he says that there are a number of regulations with regard to leave for compassionate purposes. There is the compassionate leave provision whereby a man may get leave provided undue hardship exists on the particular farm in connection with his own family. That provision has been in force and has been invoked by national defence headquarters which have had to deal with many applications. The other agricultural leave was the subject of a circular letter dated July 5, 1943, which I shall table The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr
Canadian Army

Cruickshank) asked me about this some time ago and I sent him a copy of this circular. It provides for agricultural leave for harvesting somewhat along the same lines as the leave which was provided for seeding.

Proposition after proposition and suggestion after suggestion have been made and gone over and found to be impracticable from one point of view or another. Only this morning I gave my approval to a plan which I think will work and which is just now being vested with the Department of Labour. I think it will assist the situation materially. I am not going to state its terms because there have been so many conferences and discussions with regard to it that I prefer to see it definitely settled before anything is said.

speechtext:
The letter reads:
G.O.C.-in-C., Atlantic Command,
G.O.C.-in-C., Pacific Command,
All D.Os.C.,
Commander, Petawawa Military Camp, Commander, Camp Borden Military Camp.
Agricultural leave-harvest, 1943.
It has been decided that harvest leave may be granted to such personnel of the army as can be spared, subject to the following conditions:
2.	Harvest leave may be granted under the conditions outlined below to personnel of the Canadian army (including members H.D.) serving in the following formations and units:
(i)	Personnel on the strength of H.W.E. district depots. The number granted leave to be at the discretion of the D.O.C. concerned.
(ii)	Other personnel on the strength of district depots less those awaiting dispatch to basic

training centres and those awaiting allocation after completing advanced or trades training.
(iii)	Personnel of veterans guard of Canada *who have completed individual training and who can be spared from the duties on which their units or detachments are employed.
(iv)	Personnel of units employed on operational duties less those earmarked for overseas service. Number granted leave to be at discretion of the G.O.C.-in-C. and D.O.C. concerned, but not to exceed 5 per cent of the strength of the unit concerned. Such personnel must have completed individual training before being granted leave.
3.	The general conditions under which leave for harvesting may be granted to such personnel are as follows:
(a)	Leave will not exceed six weeks duration and may be cancelled at any time.
(b)	Pay, subsistence, travelling allowance, or other allowances of any kind will not be issuable during this special leave.
(c)	Soldiers will not be entitled to medical or dental attention, hospitalization or compensation due to illness, injury or death while on leave.
(d)	Only soldiers who have experience in farm work are eligible.
(e)	Harvest leave will be limited strictly for the purpose its name implies.
4.	(a) The provisions of R.O. 1935, para. 7 (a) are not to be applied for the grant of harvest leave to personnel in operational units who are ineligible for harvest leave under the provisions of this order.
(b) The provisions of R.O. 699 (2) and (3) will not be prejudiced by the granting of this leave.
5.	The period during which personnel will require such leave will vary considerably in different parts of the country, depending on the advance of the season and weather conditions. However, all personnel must be returned to their units not later than 31 Oct., 43.
6.	The number of men granted leave at any given time will be at the discretion of general or district officers commanding concerned, who will ensure that the number who may be granted leave is limited so that the strength of units will not be unduly depleted.
7.	(a) Application will be made by the soldier concerned to his commanding officer, who, if he approves, will forward same for decision to the general or district officer commanding concerned.
(b) The conditions governing such leave are to be issued in writing to the soldier before proceeding on leave, and the address where he is to be employed is to be entered on his furlough form.
H. F. G. Letson,
Major-General,
Adjutant-General.
As I say, I prefer not to make an announcement about this further plan, which my officers have been working on, until it has been definitely settled. I have mentioned compassionate leave, and I have mentioned agricultural leave, and I have mentioned the further consideration which has been given to the matter in an endeavour to meet the situation as far as possible by providing such

Ontario Election
men as we can spare for the purposes of harvest activities. Demands have been made on the army such as have been made on no other organization in the country. There has been no such demand made upon industry, comparatively speaking. The army seems to have been considered an inexhaustible pool from which men may be obtained. Those men who are not located on the east and west coasts are in the training centres where they are necessary in order that we may have reinforcements to send overseas. Therefore it would be difficult to supply detachments of men in the central part of Canada.
I think I should mention further that we have cooperated with the Department of Labour in connection with supplying prisoners of war for special agricultural work. The house should not be surprised if it hears of the odd escape of a prisoner of war. I hope that questions will not be asked in the house about it and that it will not be regarded as a major international incident. That has almost been the attitude in connection with some prisoners of war who have temporarily escaped in the past. We feel that the situation is such that we have to do the best we can with the facilities which we have for guarding. Men are now being provided at places where it is not so easy to guard them. Where you must have one man for one prisoner you will not be saving anything in man-power. So that we have to do the best we can. In some cases the Department of Labour is assuming responsibility, and in some cases we are assuming it.
The house will be interested to know that as of June 3 there were 5,450 men on leave from Canadian active army for agricultural assistance, either by way of compassionate leave or agricultural leave. That is not counting all the men who have been granted leave in the districts without reference to headquarters, or the men granted leave under the 5th of July circular.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS - FOR VOTING BY MEMBERS OF RESERVE ARMY IN CAMPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of National Defence for the Army a question. It relates to the disfranchisement of two thousand men of the reserve army in military district No. 3, Kingston, although many men of the reserve army belong to No. 1 or No. 2 district, and in other parts of Ontario. The minister made a statement yesterday about this matter. These men and others are sure to be disfranchised on the 4th of August unless the minister takes action to postpone their departure to camp beyond next Sunday, July 25. Nomination day is only two days afterwards, and I suggest that there should be a postponement of the camp for a week and then the soldiers can vote by proxy or at an advance poll. I should like to know what the minister has done. I do not want to move the adjournment of the house to discuss the matter, but two thousand soldier civilians in the reserve army are surely going to be disfranchised unless the camps are postponed for a week.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS - FOR VOTING BY MEMBERS OF RESERVE ARMY IN CAMPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter was
brought up yesterday by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) and I intimated then that I would have an examination made of the act to ascertain whether or not these men came within the provisions of the act in regard to soldiers voting. The advice that I have received is that the act does not cover them. Therefore it is simply a matter of the men losing their votes or having the Department of National Defence make some adjustment in the absence of any provision in the act.
We have gone into the matter very carefully. You cannot simply postpone a camp of 2,700 men for a week after they have made all their arrangements with their employers and their domestic arrangements. It is not that the department has any hesitation about postponing the camp. We would gladly postpone it on twenty-four hours' notice, but we have to think of the business men- and there are a great many business men in the reserve army-who have made arrangements to leave at a particular time. We have not had one request from any business man
Ontario Election

or from any man in the ranks of the reserve army with regard to postponing their departure for the camp. Nevertheless there have been requests on both sides, and I do not want to be a party to anything, if I can possibly avoid it, which will make it more difficult for the men to exercise their franchise at an election, dominion or provincial. We have gone into the matter fully. In regard to the suggestion that we postpone the camp, we cannot postpone it so as to make it extend beyond the original termination date which is I think August 18, for the reason I have mentioned, namely, that the men have made their arrangements with their employers and their domestic and personal arrangements with regard to leave, and we therefore have to have the camp within the dates fixed because everybody has made his arrangements accordingly. If we delayed the opening of the camp until after the time for voting at the advance polls-it is not a vote by proxy but an advance poll vote- we would have to wait until after July 31, because we are advised that the advance polls will not be ready until after July 31, and that would leave one bare week before the termination date for the men to get to camp, do their training and leave to go back home. Instead of that we have decided to open the camp on the day fixed and to readjust the syllabus of training, taking into account a week-end and doing intensive training on Saturday and Sunday, which was not anticipated, in order to put in nine days' training and complete the adjusted syllabus of training on August 3, when the men can leave the camp and be back home in time to vote.
Hon. members will understand that every man who is going to a reserve camp does not have a vote. There are many boys of from seventeen to twenty-one years of age who go to the camp. In addition therefore we are giving consideration to seeing if we cannot have a special syllabus for the remainder of the days which were to be spent in the camp, for the benefit of them and any others who may want to take advantage of it. In the result this adjustment means that the men can carry out the business and domestic arrangements which they have made with respect to leave; they will still be able to vote and they will be able to complete the adjusted camp training which will be prescribed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of bill No. 137, to repeal the Japanese Treaty Act, 1913.

subtopic: JAPANESE TREATY ACT REPEAL OF STATUTE OF 1913
speechtext:
Before the bill gets second reading, may I say that I am in favour of it. So far as I can see, it is a matter of routine, the purpose being to repeal this act in consequence of the contingencies of war and the fact that Japan and Canada are now at war wdth each other. While this treaty on commercial and navigation agreements between Canada and Japan is to be repealed, I am a bit concerned that there is no evidence of any action whatsoever along this line between Russia and Japan. Of course, I know that we cannot altogether expect that, because Russia and Japan are not at war with each other. This fact is not fully realized. We think too often of the united nations, the allies, as being the British empire, the United States, China and Russia, the big four, the united nations fighting against Hitler and Mussolini. It is true that the united nations are at war with Germany and Italy, but it is not true that the united nations are at war with Japan, because Russia is one of those united nations. I do not wish to minimize the fact that the united nations are united in their efforts, but it is not true to say that they are united in their war against the axis powers. They are united against Hitler and Mussolini.
I bring this up at the moment because not so long ago Russia and Japan renewed their previous fishing treaties giving to Japan certain rights to occupy certain islands. I did not know that this bill was coming up this morning and therefore I have not my clippings before me, but I read recently that these islands are being used by Japan as weather stations which would assist her in waging war against the United States in the Pacific.	I am very much concerned
about that, because most members of parliament have received numerous requests from organizations and individuals, sometimes letters written personally and at other times circular letters, urging for instance that a second front be started against Germany in order to relieve the pressure that Germany was putting on Russia. We have received petitions signed by hundreds of people to open up a second front, to do this, that and the other, but never once have I received
Japanese Treaty Act

any communication from anyone asking that we urge that pressure be brought to bear upon Russia to assist us in respect of her relations with Japan.
The fact of the matter is that we do not know what is going to happen in the future in connection with Japan. Before the war is won I am quite certain that Japan will be our greatest enemy. I simply make these observations. I am not altogether satisfied about the alignment of nations in waging war in	the	Pacific. I say	this now becausethere will	be	no other	opportunity thissession	for	us	to express	our views in thisregard.	So	far	as the bill	itself is concerned
I am in full agreement with it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: JAPANESE TREATY ACT REPEAL OF STATUTE OF 1913
speechtext:
It is not unusual,
although not very often practised, to pass a bill of one clause, such as this, without reference to the committee of the whole. I quote from Bourinot at page 529:
It has not been uncommon in the Canadian houses to pass bills without reference to a committee of the whole. This has been almost invariably done in the case of the appropriation or supply bill and not unfrequently in the case of other bills, also founded on resolutions passed in the committee of the whole. Instances are also found in the Canadian journals of Commons bills, not based on resolutions, as well as of Senate bills, having been passed without reference to a committee of the whole. . . .
Is it the sense of the house that, after the second reading, I should put the motion for the third reading of the bill?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: JAPANESE TREATY ACT REPEAL OF STATUTE OF 1913
speechtext:
It occurred to me that if it was necessary to bring in this bill at this particular session, having in mind the fact that we declared war on Japan some time in December, 1941, there must be some reason why such a bill was not introduced at the last session of the house. I was wondering what the reason might be. Perhaps the minister can explain.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I believe I can very readily satisfy the hon. gentleman. First, I should say that the treaty provided that the subjects of the high contracting parties would have rights equal to those of their respective citizens in the two countries concerned, and that the treaty would not apply to the dominions unless they adhered to it. This dominion did adhere to it. That became then a contractual situation between Canada and Japan. That contractual situation ceased to exist when war was declared, but the form in which the statute was passed in 1913 declared that the treaty would have force of law in Canada, so that even after it ceased to have contractual effect it had statutory effect, and it was dealt with under the War
Mr. Hanstll.]
Measures Act by the defence of Canada regulations. But the War Measures Act provides that whatever is done under it will come to an end with the cessation of hostilities, so that this is necessary to repeal the statute, to prevent it from operating after the cessation of hostilities.

subtopic: JAPANESE TREATY ACT REPEAL OF STATUTE OF 1913
speechtext:
If it is necessary and advisable-I suppose it is from the minister's remarks-to pass this bill, would it not be equally appropriate and applicable to dissolve or repudiate the terms of the gentleman's agreement?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The treaty itself provided that it would come to an end twelve months after notice of repudiation given, and that notice was given in January, 1941.

subtopic: JAPANESE TREATY ACT REPEAL OF STATUTE OF 1913
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman does not get my meaning. I understand about the treaty all right. I say, why does he not take similar action as regards the gentleman's agreement with Japan-another subject altogether-by which 150 of them are allowed in every year, and which, I suppose, is still the law?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	That came to an
end, by virtue of the principles of international law, with the declaration of war. The only reason for this bill is that in 1913 they did not merely ratify the adhesion to the treaty; the statute of 1913 said in terms that the treaty would have force of law in Canada. So that even after the treaty disappears there is a statute saying that these provisions have force of law, and that is what we want to do away with by this bill. In the first place, in
clause 1, the policy of the government illustrates the general trend and policy of the government in dealing with these empire matters. This treaty is known as the Treaty of Commerce and Navigation. It was signed by the United Kingdom and Japan, as the explanatory note states, on April 3, 1911. That treaty was binding on Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the whole empire. What happened? Two years later Canada passed a separate statute, as stated in the explanatory note, declaring that the Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation signed by the United Kingdom had the force of law in Canada, and it was assented to on April 10, 1913. While I have no
Japanese Treaty Act

objection to this bill, I wish to say that war is war, and a declaration of war by Great Biitain is binding upon Canada. I do not think the minister has considered this part of the argument. China is not at war with Japan. Japan is not at war with Russia. These matters will be regulated by international law and agreement, and for us in Canada to take a separate stand from Great Britain in connection with this treaty is something I cannot understand. I do not think it is the right action to take. No doubt when war was declared upon Japan by Great Britain and then Canada, the question arose as to whether this treaty was binding any longer on the other parties to it, New Zealand, Australia and the other members of the commonwealth. I should like to ask the minister whether Australia and New Zealand, who were parties to the original treaty of commerce and navigation signed by the United Kingdom, have taken similar separate action, as in this bill, to declare that the treaty is repealed as far as those dominions are concerned. Mr. ST. LAURENT: I shall not reply to all that the hon. member has said, but I should like to make the reservation that the fact of my not replying does not mean that I agree with his views of the international relations of this country. I wish to point out to him that the plenipotentiary who signed this treaty for the United Kingdom was Sir Edward Grey, and Sir Edward Grey put his signature to a document which said in terms that it would not apply to the dominions unless on their own behalf they chose to adhere to it. Canada did choose to adhere to it, and Canada afterwards passed a statute making it law in this country. When war was declared by Canada on Japan, the treaty to which Canada had adhered and which would have had no effect upon Canada if this country had not adhered to it, was thereby abrogated and came to an end, but the Canadian statute remained on the statute book. The purpose of the bill is to remove that statute and to remove the effect thereof as to the people of Canada. As to whether anything like this has been done in Australia or New Zealand, I am not informed.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words with respect to section 28. We have just considered section 27 which states that a decision of the appeal court shall be final. Section 28 says:
No farmer shall be entitled to make more than one proposal under this act.
There has been a Ipng discussion on this bill. Away back in 1924 and 1925, when the prairie provinces were urging free trade, and all that kind of thing. I proposed to aid them all along the line by protection and The Safeguarding of Industries Act, for the benefit of the prairie farmers. It affected not only their property, but the marketing and production of their crops. During the past fifteen or sixteen years many advanced protectionist measures have been passed, some of them dealing with farm debt, others with the farms themselves, the appliances used on the farm, production, distribution and marketing of the crop and so on. When the prairies veered around to protection, after seeing the great injury which had been done by the opposite policy, I pointed out that there should be a national policy to apply protection to all Canada's ills. I am not opposing adequate measures to take care of this problem of farm debt on the prairies and the hardship caused thereby; my point is that any measure should have a greater scope and be reciprocal and apply aid to all Canada to protect equities. A measure such as this should not be brought in during the dying days of parliament when it cannot receive the consideration it deserves. It has to go to another place and we do not know how it will fare there. In my opinion it might be well to let it stand over for a year. This measure is onesided; it is not reciprocal.
A proper national policy of protection would benefit not only the market gardener and the farmer, but the artisan and the industrial worker. Then it would be worthy of the name of protection. A measure such as this ought to be applied to all. On April 17, 1925, I said that protection is a great economic question of principle and of patriotism, and of life and death to Canadians. The big interests, who seek to grab all the benefits of protection for themselves, are its worst friends, and do the great movement little good. It should not be a manufacturers' question, or a banking question, or a grain growers' question, or a combine question, or a monopoly question at all. Protection should be brought up to date to meet changed conditions, and extended. Protection will make for a better Canada, and a happier and more contented people, with work plentiful; it will make

Farmers' Creditors Act
Canada a country fit for heroes who have fought for Canada to live and die in, instead of being driven to join the exodus.
Instead of a measure of protection to cover our fishermen, our industrial workers in the central provinces, and our farmers or. the prairies, and the Pacific toilers and the equity in their homes, we have a one-sided protection measure. I say that this will only cause untold hardship for those who will have to help pay for it. This bill is only half-baked to begin with. They talk about fifty per cent of the farmers on the prairies having no debt on their farms, and we must not forget that there are many widows and others who have invested their money in farm mortgages on the prairies while others have taken out insurance policies or have bought loan or trust company bonds. Their security in these companies may be wiped out. If this principle is to be adopted it will cause wide differences of opinion and disunity in Canada.
I have no objection to attempting to relieve this very serious state of affairs to which my hon. friends to my left referred yesterday, but I plead for equality of treatment to other native industries and the industrial population. This is a form of state socialism-for some, and not for others. If you are going to adopt it you might just as well say that there will be no proper protection for the policyholders in these insurance companies, whose assets will go down and may be seriously affected. In the dying days of parliament we should not pass this measure. During the last few days of the session we cannot give a matter like this proper consideration. If they are going to ask for more than is in the bill, or for more than is proper, it will only cause trouble. I doubt whether some of the clauses of these measures are constitutional in view of the decision of the privy council, on provincial farm debt matters. It will cause wide differences of opinion in the other provinces of the confederation.
You, Mr. Chairman, were once the head in Ontario of a fine municipality in an agricultural community, and you know that people in Ontario consider that province the forgotten province. We have not received the same treatment that others have. I think the government should consider widening this bill, or possibly let it stand over for a year and then provide a wider measure of relief for those who are not covered at all and for those who should be covered, so as to have real national protection to the real estate of all our people and the holding or the equities in their homes.

The minister says that there will be less inconsistency when the courts deal with these cases, that there has been inconsistency in the decisions of the boards. There may be more consistency by the courts in dealing with technical and legal aspects, but the trouble with this legislation, and the reason I am so much opposed to the courts handling it, is that the courts will have to be more than legal interpreters; they will have to be experts on farm management to decide on the ability of the farmer to pay and on the productive capacity of his farm. Most men on the bench are no more competent to decide these two questions than are men you might pick off the streets. One of the reasons why the boards of review were so inconsistent in the early stages was that they had had no experience in that work, but years of experience in handling these cases gave them more information and a better insight into farm management. That is why in later years their decisions were much better. The minister has not advanced any reason why the courts will be any more consistent in their decisions. It is true that in dealing with technical and legal aspects they may be, bu* when it comes to deciding on a farmers ability to pay and on the productive capacity of his land, I think the courts will have to do what the boards of review did-just feel their way by an experimental process of trial and error. They will be just as cautious as the boards of review were at first, but as they get more experience in farm management they will be able to make more equitable adjustments. In view of that fact I think 
the minister would have been well advised to provide, as proposed in the draft bill, a probationary period of five years, not that there should be adjustments from time to time and no finality but that in this probationary period of five years of experimentation the farmer and creditor would be able to see how the arrangement was working out, and if it was not working out satisfactorily the matter could be reviewed'.

I do not think that would
have a good effect at all. I think if the judges approached the question with the idea that they were instituting a probationary settlement, then to begin with the settlement would not be as good or as careful. I think the fact that there is to be finality about the settlement imposes on the judge an obligation to take care which would not exist if the settlement were to be a mere preliminary or probationary one. The creation of an appeal court is a factor making for consistency which does not exist in the present system. I do not want to be misunderstood as criticizing the present boards of review, because they have done a lot of very fine work, but there is something in what the hon. member for Lake Centre says, that when administrative boards have the final say, they are likely to be a little more dogmatic-I was going to say arbitrary-than when there is an appeal from their decisions. It is a criticism of a lot of our war-time controls, and there is something in it. It is probably a human quality to be decisive and at times dogmatic and, with some persons, arbitrary, if there is no appeal from their decisions. The fact that a minister of the crown has over him the government, that he cannot just say yes or no and tell everybody to take the consequences, but that there is a government which in the final analysis can overrule him, has a beneficial effect on the minister. Sometimes it slows him up and in time of war one sometimes wishes that his voice was the only voice. But I think consistency in his decisions is probably assured to a certain extent by the fact that there is a superior body over him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I wish to move an amendment to this section. The three main features of the amendment are: first, that the provisions of the section shall not apply to compositions, extensions of time, or schemes of arrangement which have been approved by the court or confirmed by the board of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934. The section as it stands would unsettle certain settlements on which the farmer probably has the right to rely. It will apply only for the future; it will apply only to compositions, extensions of time or schemes of arrangement approved by the court under the act now before the house. That is the first change that is proposed in the section. The second is that the period of five years be reduced to three years. The third is that such additional amount as the court thinks should be paid for the benefit of 72537-327
the creditors is to be paid into court instead of directly to the creditors. There is a fourth; that is, that the amount is not to be payable to one holder of the security on the said land, or to the vendor or assignee of the vendor under the agreement for sale, but is to be applied by the court for any holder of security on the said land, or the vendor or assignee of the vendor under the agreement for sale.
The need for this section is indicated by experience. I have before me a list of cases in which the dominion government was the secured creditor; I suppose there are hundreds of cases like this in which private mortgagees or vendors were the secured creditors. I have not gone over those at all but have had selected, I think at random-I am not just sure on what basis they were selected- eighteen cases in which the crown was the creditor, through the soldier settlement board. This is what happened in those cases; I shall take perhaps the most outstanding one, though it may not be. The original debt was $6,586.59. The date of reduction of the debt was May 9, 1938. The reduced debt was S3,500.	On October 20, 1939, less than
eighteen months later, the debtor sold the property for $6,850. Hon. gentlemen will take note of what happened there, and I would ask them to put themselves in the position of trustees for the taxpayers of Canada. As holder of the security on that property the soldier settlement board were compelled to reduce the amount of their debt against that farmer by $3,000, from $6,586.59 to $3,500; they were compelled to do so under the provisions of an act the object of which, as stated in the preamble, was to retain the farmer on the land as an efficient producer. Within eighteen months that farmer who was thus enabled to remain on the land as an efficient producer sold the property for $6,850. Of course the crown took that loss of $3,000 and the farmer got the benefit of the difference.	.
The theory of this section, the principle underlying it, is that if something definite of that kind takes place, showing clearly that the court erred, that the purposes of the act were frustrated and that there should not have been any such reduction at all, the farmer should make some of that money available for the satisfaction of the persons who had security on the land. The section therefore provides that the farmer cannot, within three years after this settlement- which, it must be borne in mind, is made for the purpose of keeping him on the land as an efficient producer-sell the land without getting leave of the court. The court may

Farmers' Creditors Act

impose conditions, one of which may be that such sum as the court thinks fit will be paid into court for the benefit of those who have security on the land.
That is one case. There is another case on this list in which apparently the farmer sold the land within six months. The original debt was $4,236.27. The date of reduction was May 5, 1939. The reduced debt was $2,000. On November 7, 1939, he sold the land for $3,040. Under the proposed section it would be necessary if he changed his mind about staying on the land, which was what happened in this case, to come to the court and say, "I am going to sell this land, for which I am going to get $3,040. Your $4,000 was cut down to $2,000. I want to know on what terms I can sell the land," and the terms may include the condition that some part of the money be paid into court for the benefit of those holding security on the land.	Those holders of
security might include municipalities who had taxes owing, or anyone else who had an interest in the land.
The proposed legislation is based to a large extent on a section of the New Zealand act which is very much like this. I have no information as to subsequent legislation in New Zealand, but in 1936 they passed an act which had an emergency application, just like the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. It enabled farmers and others to apply within a limited period, within a year or two, for a reduction of their debts, and it provided that if anyone sold the land before January 1, 1941, which was about four years after the expiration of the act, they must do this very thing. I have the provisions of the New Zealand act before me. I do not say that we are doing this because New Zealand did it; we are doing this because one of the features of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act that has always shocked a good many people is that debtors could go to a board of review, sometimes with a sale in view, and avail themselves of the provisions of an act designed to keep efficient producers on the land, in order to get a substantial write-down of their mortgages. Then, shortly afterwards, they could sell the land for an amount very considerably in excess of the sum to which the debt was reduced.

33. (1) Where any debt secured on the land owned by a farmer or owing or payable by a farmer under an agreement for sale of any land has been reduced under any composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement approved or confirmed by the court under this act, the farmer shall not, except with the leave of the court granted upon such terms and conditions as the court thinks fit, sell or otherwise dispose of such land or any part thereof or his interest therein within a period of three years after the date on which the composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement was approved or confirmed.
(2) The conditions imposed by the court upon granting leave to any farmer to make any such sale or other disposition may include a condition that such portion of the selling price or other consideration, as the court deems equitable, having regard to all the circumstances and in particular to any improvements made to the land since the date of such approval or confirmation, shall become payable into the court in such manner and within such time as the court directs, and shall be applied by the court for the benefit of any holder of security on the said land or the vendor or assignee of the vendor under the agreement for sale.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I should like if possible at this stage to have the discussion kept within the limits of the bill.

Farmers' Creditors Act

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I shall be glad to do that. The lion., member for Peace River is much alarmed lest any opposition to this legislation may result in its defeat. I want to tell him that he can be absolutely certain that legislation that is as favourable to the creditor class as this is will go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman surely does not say that the creditor class is helped by this legislation. Suppose we had no legislation and a creditor in the western provinces had the same rights as a creditor in the other provinces, would he not have much wider rights than he will have as a result of this legislation? This legislation gives nothing to the creditor class; it takes away from them.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: This legislation takes the power away from the boards of review and gives it to the courts. Apparently these boards of review have been much too sympathetic and much too generous to the debtor class, according to what has been said by many in this house and outside the house. I think the strongest objection that has been taken by various members is that the boards of review have been so generous, or as the minister says, so inconsistent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman continues to say that this legislation was brought in because the boards of review were too favourable to the debtors. That is not the reason for the legislation, and the hon. gentleman should accept the reasons I have repeatedly given. That is not one of them.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I am stating
that the effect of this legislation is to take power away from the boards of review and give it to the courts. If this legislation were not here, the boards of review would continue to function. The minister has been arguing all along for finality. There is to be no revision once a proposal has been filed, as far as the farmer is concerned. If the farmer is not able to meet the terms of the composition, there is to be no revision; there is to be no adjustment; he goes into bankruptcy unless he gets a postponement. The only group that can get a revision'-that is what this amounts to-is to be the creditor group, in the event of the debtor selling his farm for more than the total amount of the debt against it. In other words, the only place where the principle of finality is to be dispensed with is the place where the legislation might work out in the interests of the farmer debtor. The principle for which the minister has been contending for two days is being violated by this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I want finality where the
parties concerned abide by the intent and spirit of the bill. This bill provides for finality where the man stays on the land for three years after the settlement. The object of the legislation is to enable him to stay on the land as an efficient producer. If he does so, there is every finality so far as he is concerned and so far as the creditor is concerned. But if he does not, if he gets a write-down so that he can stay on the land and then, as many have done, sells his land for a very considerable increase in value and gets off the land, he should come back to the court and say, "That was not the basis; I have changed my mind, I want to sell the land." The court may then impose a condition having regard to all the circumstances. That is the spirit and intent of the legislation, and I argue for that.
I point out another consideration, perhaps not strictly on this point, and that is that there is a considerable class who will take advantage of this, and the largest class, I take it. There is a second chance for the debtors who had their proposals confirmed before January 1, 1939-not all of them but those who come within the other conditions of the legislation. But the creditor does not have a second chance.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: There may be circumstances under which the land is being sold not because of the choice of the debtor at all. The debtor may die and his widow be unable to carry on the farm; having no grown-up son, she is compelled by economic circumstances to dispose of the land. In that case she will take the case to the court and have to give the creditor whatever opportunity he can avail himself of to get part of the proceeds when she is disposing of her farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That is correct, and I do not see anything wrong with that at all. I have a different point of view from my hon. friend. It may be my background, my environment or something like that, but I have seen people who take their savings and invest them in a mortgage on a neighbouring farm, say a mortgage of $2,000. Sometimes they had worked hard to accumulate those savings over a period of years. It would seem to me that if the farm were sold for three or four or five thousand dollars the person who lent his savings on the security of a mortgage should get back his $2,000 if the farm is sold. I do not see any reason why he should not. To propound these new partnership theories, this theory of heads I win and tails you lose, seems to me to take away the
Farmers' Creditors Act

whole foundation of our present contractual system. Some hon. gentlemen opposite would like to write out of contracts the contractual feature. I cannot as Minister of Finance agree with that. The dominion government has to live up to its contracts; each one of us individually has to live up to his contract, and apart from recognizing the emergency feature here and going as far as is necessary to meet it, I cannot agree to go any farther.
If a man comes in under this legislation, which is designed to keep him on the land as an efficient producer, and has his mortgage written down from $5,000 to $3,000 and his estate is able to get $5,000 for the land, my hon. friend thinks it is a terrible thing that the creditor should be paid off the full amount of his mortgage. What is there wrong about that? The money was advanced on the land. There was a contract to pay back the amount of the mortgage. What social value is impaired there? What harm will it do to the nation? The mortgage, we will say, had to be written down to keep the farmer on the land, and the farmer stayed on the land until he died, perhaps a year or two afterwards. Then it turns out that the land is worth a whole lot more than the mortgage. Why should there be anything wrong about the present owner of the land being obliged to go back to the court and get permission to sell on terms that will preserve so far as possible the contractual feature in the contract?

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The minister asks what is wrong with the illustration he gave, and I notice that he got support from the hon. member for Rosedale. Their outlook is identical, and the minister will, I am sure, be relieved on that score. The minister states the case of a man whose debts are $5,000. The man has probably paid back in principal and interest thousands of dollars already. Then he has his debt written down to $3,000 by the court, which recognizes in that adjustment the value of the farm and that the farmer has already paid back large sums of money and has worked on the farm to break it and clear it and has some equity in it. Now, says the minister, if that land is sold by the estate for $5,000, why should the farmer's widow or his heirs get $2,000? That is what it amounts to. Why should the creditor have to put up with $3,000, he asks, when there are $5,000 of proceeds? Why should not the wages of money come first? Why should not the wages of labour simply be written off? That is what the minister is saying. The minister is saying that the wages of capital are the only wages that are to be sacrosanct, that the only contract is a 
property contract, and that the money that has already been paid out by the farmer and his famity and all the work they have put in on the farm are not to be regarded at all. That is his whole assumption. If the proceeds from the farm amount to $5,000 the creditor should take it all, and the man's family who have already paid in so much and have done so much work on the farm go without anything. What is wrong with that, the minister asks? There is a great deal wrong with it. There is a complete failure to recognize the farmer's equity and the	hard work	that	has been done	byhundreds of farming people all across this country. If the minister is going to argue along that line there is no common ground upon which we can argue, because in his eyes the only sacred thing is the obligation to the people who have invested their money. We are trying to get the minister to recognize that when there is a loss, as there has	been a loss in	western Canada	ofmillions of dollars because of the depression and drought, that loss must be shared equally by both sides, and the labour that the farmer has	put in and	the	payments that have
already been made by him warrant him in having some return from the proceeds of that farm. He has as much right to it as the creditor.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I just want to say to my	hon. friend,	who	comes from the	old
country like myself, that one thing that has made the British people great is sanctity of contracts. My hon. friend has the thing in reverse. He is trying to tell the house that the man who lends his money is a scoundrel and that the chap who will not pay back what he owes is a hero.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Not at ali.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I was always taught, as I am sure my hon. friend was, that if you borrow money and spend it foolishly you must pay it back just the same. I think that is fundamental.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
And you
would apply it to the farmer in this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I certainly would. If he gets a mortgage for S6,000 written down to $3,000 and then sells his farm for $6,000, a part of those proceeds belong to the person who lent him the money. To destroy thrift is to destroy civilization. I know hundreds of working people in communities all over this country who have saved a few hundred dollars by - hard work and thrift and are lending it out, and we must have regard for these people and their savings. I am not

Farmers' Creditors Act
talking of the big loan companies but of the hundreds of working people one meets in every community. In fairness you must have some regard for the other fellow. Of course we all know that through hard circumstances a person may at times be unable to meet his obligations.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

Nothing in this act or in any composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangements approved by the court or confirmed by the board of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, or approved or confirmed by the court under this act, relating to the debts or affairs of a purchaser of land, or of an assignee of a purchaser of land, under agreement for sale from the director of soldier settlement, shall be deemed to limit or restrict the powers of the said director. . . .

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Will the minister give consideration to making the rate of interest four per cent instead of five?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I do not know that there should be such a great reduction as that. It is only in the cases where the rate of interest exceeds seven per cent that this section applies. This is taken from the old act; it is to apply to those high rates of interest where the interest rate collectible is more than seven per cent; then, by tendering the money, the mortgagor can get it down to five per cent.	*

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I want the minister to consider reducing it to four per cent.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Does that mean that all interest rates will be cut down to five per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No, it does not mean that at all.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I think the minister ought to give some consideration to a provision, either this section or another, dealing with the question of interest rates. This deals only with the case where the farmer has been paying more than seven per

Farmers' Creditors Act
cent; he is now given a new proposal under which the interest rate will be five per cent, but if he has been paying six or seven he may continue to pay six or seven. The minister will agree that a study made of western conditions by the Sirois commission showed that agriculture in the west cannot pay a return of six or seven per cent. One of the things which has ruined western Canada, as has been said repeatedly by those who have examined conditions there, is high rates of interest. Over a period of years one of the reasons that farmers have been under such a burden of debt is the high rate of interest, compounded year after year. The minister would be well advised to consider fixing a maximum rate. If he is not prepared to cut it all to five per cent, he could set a maximum of, say, six, but as it is now it really means that if a man pays seven he will keep on paying seven, and if he pays six he will keep on paying six. I do not think that on back debts the average farm to-day will support six or seven per cent interest. What a number of hon. members who keep acting as though we were trying to deprive somebody of his just due do not realize is that you cannot get blood out of stone, that if the farm does not produce a crop you cannot get a return from it, and in a country where, at least in some parts, the average of crops is only two or three good crops out of five, a farm will not support a family, meet running costs, and pay a high rate of interest on debt, particularly on a back debt which has piled up in addition to more recent debt. The minister would be well advised to consider a provision that in these compositions there will be a maximum rate of interest, and that that maximum should be not more than five per cent. I would go even lower, but I think five per cent is the very most that the average farmer's farm will support on back debt.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Why does the minister consider that some should pay 7 per cent and others have their rate reduced to 5 per cent? Why have two rates of interest? I know that some have paid it over the years, but we are now making an adjustment, and surely when the minister is permitting some to come down to 5 per cent, all should be brought down to 5. I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that probably the rate should be down lower than five in order to make it possible for the farmer to pay, but since the minister has the rate here at 5 per cent I suggest that all should be cut to 5 per cent, because, as has been pointed out 72537-328
by the hon. member for Weybum, it is just impossible for the farmer to meet contractual obligations if they are too onerous. It is useless to put an impossible proposition before a farmer and expect him to live up to it. You may sell his land and put him off the farm, but you will not make him pay, because payment is utterly impossible. In all fairness the minister should cut the rate of interest to 5 per cent; that should be the highest rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The rate of interest charged by the Canadian farm loan board on first mortgages is 5 per cent, and on second mortgages, I believe, 6 per cent. Something depends on risk when one is trying to ascertain what is the appropriate rate of interest. This section merely provides that a person can get his interest on an existing mortgage down to 5 per cent if he is in a position to tender the mortgagee the value of the mortgage.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: He would have to tender him everything?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Back payments of principal and interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That is right. I do not know of any use to which the section has ever been put. I do not know that we would be justified in putting the rate any lower. We might, perhaps, put the penal rate in there; that is what the 4 per cent would be, because it would just be punishing the mortgage company for not releasing a mortgagor when he is tendering the principal and interest.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: You could bring it down to 5 per cent without any penal provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Well, 5 per cent is the rate in the section. It is the rate of interest charged by the government itself-the Canadian farm loan board. Answering the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, I do not think there is any necessity of changing the terms of the section. The hon. members for Weyburn and Bow River have raised another point, as to whether we should give a statutory direction here to judges that they would have to reduce the rate of interest to 5 per cent on mortgages in all cases before them. As a matter of fact, in practice the boards of review in Alberta and Saskatchewan, I believe, have been pretty generally reducing the rate of interest to 5 per cent in the case of applications to them. I think that is the case in Saskatchewan, and it was the case in Alberta; perhaps it is now.

Farmers' Creditors Act

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Why should not this conform with that practice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: This does not give them any direction one way or the other; neither did the other legislation give them any direction one way or the other. The theory of the legislation is that they will do what is appropriate to the individual case. However, the boards in Saskatchewan did take the view that in no case should anyone who could qualify for an adjustment pay more than five per cent. In many cases they did not think they could qualify for an adjustment, they were not entitled to any relief, they could carry their existing obligations without much trouble; in those cases I do not think they granted any relief. But where a case was made for not being able to meet their obligations and a board did make an adjustment of interest, they adjusted it down to five per cent. I think it is a matter for the tribunal, rather than for a statutory direction. I am afraid that a statutory direction would be too rigid. Maybe the proposal went farther; maybe it was that all interest on farm mortgages should be reduced to five per cent. That is a matter of amendment to the Interest Act, and very large considerations are involved. I do not think we should take that up now; I do not believe it really belongs in this measure.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
But the
dominion government is the proper authority to state what the rate of interest should be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Yes, we have jurisdiction over interest.

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
And it would relieve the judges of that responsibility
if we definitely stated in the act that the rate of interest on mortgages should be five per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: What about the rate of interest on second mortgages; should it be higher?

subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
