Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the house, but I feel there are one or two things which should be said before the bill is given third reading. In its present form we do not feel this measure will be sufficient to deal effectively with the problems of western Canada. We have spoken at some length on the debate on second reading, and there has been considerable discussion in committee of the whole, on which occasions we have pointed *out what we considered to be the main deficiencies. Very briefly I enumerate them:
1.	We object to the section which states that two-thirds of the debt of the farmer must have been incurred prior to 1935 in order that the farmer may be in a position to make a proposal. We say that that date should be put forward at least to 1939.
2.	We object to the sections which fail to provide legal counsel for farmers when they [DOT]come before the courts, or when they make appeals.
3.	We object to the bill on the ground that it fails to treat farm debts as a recurring problem.

The western debt conference represented not only the three provincial governments in western Canada, but represented also the majority of farm organizations in the west. By no stretch of the imagination can it be said that the western debt conference dealt with this subject as a political football. I would ask the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards) if he would suggest that the premier of Saskatchewan, or the Liberal government in that province, dealt with this matter as a political football. I would ask him whether the premier of Manitoba dealt with it as a political football. And if neither of those two did, then I think we must agree that the premier of Alberta did not deal with it in that way.
As a result of the deliberations of that conference a bill was submitted to the federal government on March 15 of this year. It is our submission that that bill deals far more effectively with western debt problems than does the one before the house. It has been suggested that if this bill were brought in line with the one suggested by the conference there might be some opposition in another place. I would ask this: Why should we allow any archaic body to set aside the will of the representatives of the people of Canada?
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) I move in amendment:
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole, with instructions that they have power to amend it in such respects as will make it conform with the terms of the proposed "Act to Provide for the Adjustment and Settlement of the Debts of Farmers" submitted by the western debt conference to the dominion government on March 15, 1943.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSOLIDATION OP ARRANGEMENT ACT OP 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out the following features of the amendment, which 1 have not seen until this moment. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) takes three objections to the bill. The first is that it should not be confined to those, two-thirds of whose debts were incurred before May 1, 1935. The second objection is that the date should be January 1, 1939. That is really one point, namely that the date should be moved from May 1, 1935 to January 1, 1939.

Farmers' Creditors Act
As I said in the debate, I believe the present provisions of the bill will provide for the overwhelming bulk of the cases. I believe experience will show that in that respect I am right. I do not anticipate that there will be any rush to the courts by the farmers of western Canada, under present conditions, to avail themselves of the provisions of the bill.
I believe that those cases in respect of which relief is really required will be embraced within the provisions of the bill, which confines such relief to those, two-thirds of whose debts were incurred before May 1, 1935.
I would point out, however, that even if some person who should have relief cannot come under that provision, he has the protection of the order in council. I believe the situation is such that we can see what the experience is under the bill as at present drafted. That really is one objection, that the date should be moved from May, 1935, to January 1, 1939. I have nothing further to say as to the reasons why I prefer to retain the date of May 1, 1935.
The second point, which was described as the third point by the hon. member, is that the bill fails to recognize the problem of debt as a recurring problem. That is inconsistent with the hon. member's first point, because it really means that there should not be any date at all, and that debts, whenever they are incurred, should be taken into account in qualifying an applicant for eligibility for relief. There is an inconsistency in those two positions. I suggest the hon. member should have put his case in this form: "I urge point No. 2; but if that cannot be done, then in the alternative I urge point No. 1." That is the only way in which the hon. member could make his contention consistent.
In regard to point No. 2, namely, that the debt problem should be regarded as a recurring one, several times in the course of the debate I have stated the reasons why I do not think this parliament should adopt the principle that debts, past, present and future, should be reducible by tribunals without applicants being under any obligation to divest themselves of their assets. I have pointed out that that is not the case with regard to the other provinces. It is not so with respect to any other class of Canadians, nor does it apply in any other country, so far as I have been able to ascertain.
That was not the principle of the debt adjustment act of the western provinces and it was not the principle of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. It would be a very serious principle to adopt. If we were to adopt that principle for western Canada, we certainly should adopt it for eastern Canada. There is
no reason in the world for making that a sectional feature of our legislation. There is reason for making the present legislation sectional because it recognizes a prairie farm emergency which has passed, but the results of which have not been obviated.
If we are to lay down the principle that when the farmers of Canada borrow money they are not obliged to pay it back, even though they have security out of which to pay it back-if some court or tribunal says that they do not have to pay it back-if we are to lay down that principle, it must be a universal principle applicable all over Canada. If it is applicable to farmers, I think there are other occupations to which it should be applicable. It would be a serious step for this parliament to take.
Summing up the hon. gentleman's argument for his amendment, the only consistent way in which he could put it is that we should treat debt as a recurring problem. I have stated the objections to that, and I think they are serious. He could even have gone on and said, "I think your date is wrong, it should! have been January 1, 1939, instead of May 1, 1935." That is a matter of judgment, but I think experience will show that the legislation as drafted reasonably meets the situation.

speechtext:
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to provide for the promotion of the physical fitness of the people of Canada, the constitution of a national council on physical fitness to carry out such purpose, the establishment of a special account in the consolidated revenue fund out of moneys appropriated by parliament and the disbursement from such account of moneys required for the purposes of the act, including grants to the provinces under agreements that may be entered into.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL FOR THE PROMOTION OF PHYSICAL FITNESS
speechtext: I think perhaps that this is as appropriate a time as any for the minister to make a detailed statement with respect to the provisions and objects of the legislation to be founded upon this resolution,

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL FOR THE PROMOTION OF PHYSICAL FITNESS
speechtext:
I shall be pleased to make a brief introduction by way of explaining this resolution, which is

antecedent to a bill which has been on the Votes and Proceedings in the possession of hon. gentlemen for several days. The bill is printed and ready for distribution, This legislation is based upon a recommendation by the select committee on social security which was submitted to the house a few days ago. It is the result of careful consideration by that committee. Excellent evidence was given before the committee by gentlemen from the universities of McGill, Toronto and McMaster, and also by one gentleman who is interested in this work in a practical way in British Columbia.
Hon. gentlemen will recall that before the war there w*as a pronounced movement on the European continent in favour of such measures. Czechoslovakia and the Scandinavian countries had national fitness programmes. This matter was brought forward by the League of Nations in 1936, and in 1937 the British government sent an official commission to Europe to investigate the various systems in effect. In 1937 the health committee of the League of Nations sent representations to the various members of the league asking that they set up national bodies to deal with physical fitness. Those representations were duly conveyed at that time to the government of Canada, but no action was taken before the war. Schemes such as this are in effect in Australia, and to a certain extent in Great Britain and the United States of America.
The proposal in the bill, which follows the resolution, is to establish a national council of physical fitness. The grant proposed to the provinces is $225,000 on a fifty-fifty basis, and $25,000 for national administration. It is proposed that each province shall have a member on the council of physical fitness, and the national director will be the only paid official. The others will be entitled to their expenses when attending meetings dealing with the programme. The programme is not one of compulsion or coercion in the slightest degree ; it is one of cooperation. In the first place there will be cooperation with other departments of government. The Department of Labour is now carrying on vocational training and has a recreational scheme under its selective service wdng. There will also be cooperation with the provincial governments and with voluntary agencies and individuals who are carrying out work along these lines.
It is apparent to everyone that in the last two or three years in particular we have had brought home to us the fact that the standard of physical fitness among our people has not been as high as we should have liked it to be. The figures with regard to enlistments have

Physical Fitness Act
brought that fact strongly home to us. Voluntary organizations have been doing wonderful work in Canada in recent years along these lines. Some of the provinces have been doing work on their own, especially the two farthest west provinces, Alberta and British Columbia. As I say, these provinces have been giving consideration to this problem.
It is not a very comprehensive measure but at least it is a beginning; perhaps tall oaks may from little acorns grow. The legislation is non-contentious and non-controversial and has had wonderful support in the committee on social security. I hope that it will receive the same support from hon. members in the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL FOR THE PROMOTION OF PHYSICAL FITNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the scope of the motion of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) is a most commendable one. But to carry it out efficiently is another matter. In Canada we are naturally a hardy people, but the war has brought to light great defects in our physical education and our educational system generally. The resolution means that Canada at last will now have to embark on a system of national education concurrently with the provinces. National education goes back to the days of Thomas Arnold in 1840, when a great campaign for a revival of learning was conducted by this authority on education. He believed that book learning came last and that what came first was love of country, service and sacrifice to one's fellows, patriotism and the protection of one's country, and that Christian principles and physical fitness were second. He, as I said, placed religious and moral principles first, gentlemanly conduct and patriotism second, and intellectual ability last.
There has been a great change in thought of the people of the British empire as a result of the war. The war brought to light that a large number of our young people were not physically fit; it showed the need of a national movement to promote physical fitness among men, women and children, and our whole system of education from elementary schools to the universities seemed to have been lacking and deficient.
I think this resolution would be better if it provided that grants should be made to the municipalities instead of to the provinces. The money in turn could be distributed among boards of education, public and separate schools, primary and secondary schools and the universities. Some provinces have a different system of distribution from others, so that I think it would be better to make the grants directly to the municipalities. But certainly the

physical fitness movement should be national in scope. Everybody is familiar with the sight of several hundreds of spectators watching a small group of players in some particular sport, but the universities have changed all that and established an extra-mural curriculum under which every student will have to take some compulsory training in physical exercises and sport. The result is that at McGill and Toronto universities ninety-nine per cent of the students will now be taking compulsory physical exercises and taking part in extra-mural sports, the only exceptions being those who are excused on a doctor's certificate.
I think this department should also promote, foster and encourage all kinds of sport. We have had no national policy on sports since the war began, no well thought-out plan in relation to the war. We are now entering the fifth year of the war, and the government should, before parliament adjourns, issue a considered statement in relation to the function of sport in view of the new rules and regulations of national selective service and the further reduction in railway travel for non-essential purposes. Such a statement should cover amateur sport, to which we owe so much in this war, as shown by the great numbers of amateur sportsmen who have enlisted and gone overseas, some of whom have been killed. It should also cover professional sport; the joint military forces schedules of sport contests, and their military leagues, and the wide travelling of some from coast to coast that is involved; also national civilian and military contests of all kinds. Will anything be done in war time to reduce the cost of tickets to some of these contests and scheduled games? I believe in the promotion of sport and should like to see it made a part of this important resolution. Canada has excelled in this war, as it did in the last, largely through sportsmanship of all kinds and branches. Our young people rushed to the colours, and the first to go were those who had had cadet training and the best of those who had engaged in all sport. It was a retrograde step to abolish cadet training. Then there were those who enlisted early in the war who had taken part in sports and all kinds of games. I have been a warm supporter of sports, but now that we are in the fifth year of the war there should be a national statement from the government to clear the air as to what shall be done to finish the war and then what shall be done afterwards.
True it is that the secondary schools have promoted physical fitness by physical exercises and sports and games. They have coaches in every branch of sport who give their time free and their money and lend their cars
Physical Fitness Act

for this purpose, teaching the young people how to play up and play the game, how to play for the love of the game and develop the team spirit. What has been done in the primary and secondary schools of this country and universities and by sports clubs in the last ten or fifteen years has been most commendable, and I hope the minister will not be unmindful of the very important work that has been done along these lines by the secondary schools, by the public and separate schools and private schools and universities. I am a warm supporter of amateur sport, which should be continued throughout the war. As to professional sport, professional baseball is played mostly by Americans, but the Toronto team has given splendid leadership in the Toronto district. The work of the Toronto baseball club haS been most commendable. They admit soldiers free to all the games. Our football, hockey and other teams have also done excellent service at home and overseas in the war, and should be continued in the usual way. Some small abuses have crept in; for instance, those in some of the forces are transported from Vancouver to Halifax to play in possibly only one game. The government promised a statement on this matter of national sport in relation to the war long ago, and I hope they will look into the whole question. I believe the people of Canada will support the government in continuing sport for sport's sake during the war.
Some people say we are fighting this war for two purposes: One is to defend Christianity, and they do not tell the youth of the country what Christianity is; and the second is to protect the British empire, without telling you what the British empire is and what it has meant down the ages. The teachers in our schools are excellent, but rules and regulations hamper them.
We have always been fond of games, and I hope there will be a united effort from coast to coast to make this national physical fitness campaign a success. The medical profession has urged it for years. Physical fitness has always on a large scale been an important part of the work of secondary schools and universities, and of our community clubs. A school should not be judged by examinations only in studies, but by patriotism and service for others.
As I said before, I think the funds, instead of being distributed to the provinces, should go to the municipalities and boards of education, urban and suburban. It is well known that there has been a heavy burden on the taxpayers for education. The tax rate in the city I come from is high. We have a tax burden of $12,000,000 a year now, and in this work the municipalities should receive some

federal assistance. After all is said and done, one of the mistakes of the fathers of confederation was not to give the dominion and the provinces concurrent jurisdiction in the matter of education. The result has been that medicine, science and all these other things that are so essential to physical fitness have had little or no support from the federal government, with the awful cost to our man-power in the war.
I commend the minister generally and I hope that before this part of the session is over, there will be some statement regarding national sport, along the lines I have suggested, to clear the air for the remainder of the war and after it.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL FOR THE PROMOTION OF PHYSICAL FITNESS
speechtext:
I have no desire to take up much of the time of the house at this stage of the resolution, but I believe that the people of Canada generally will agree with the objects that lie behind it. As to the means by which they are to be achieved, that may be another matter. In any event, that will be made apparent at a later stage when we are discussing the bill.
The minister referred to physical fitness as disclosed by the examinations that took place as men and women entered the various armed services of the country. That was a revealing bit of statistics and one which no doubt had a considerable bearing and influence upon the committee that dealt with this particular subject. The fact that the social security committee largely agreed with, and perhaps were unanimous in bringing in, such a bill indicates I believe the necessity for parliament keeping abreast of public sentiment on health matters generally.
Most of us who have observed public movements in this field know that the people are conscious of health measures, and we know that this movement has been considerably accelerated in recent years. One only needs to note that there are large numbers of people in Canada to-day who are reading those columns that discuss the health of the individual. In addition to that the insurance companies, who are of course interested in rates of mortality, have taken it upon themselves, in their several private capacities, to acquaint the public with certain important features of public health. All these matters have received the conscious consideration of the public and what we have before us is a logical move in the direction of certain definite ends which the public has in mind.
One of the things which of course this government as well as the country will have to take into earnest consideration is that part and parcel of any physical fitness scheme is

Physical Fitness Act
the question, of nutrition, in which both the minister and his department are interested, and that involves the question of the means by which our citizens of all classes shall have the right in the years to come to a sufficient income with which to purchase the proper kinds of food in order that their health may be preserved. I do not think that this resolution should pass without some reference being made to that particular point, because I am convinced that some at least of our difficulties come to us from those days when the country was not as affluent as it is at the present time. In my part of the country I had a good deal of experience with men and women who found it necessary to go on relief. Those are days which none of us want to see again.
I would emphasize that hand in hand with any solution that is proposed for the whole problem of physical fitness is the corollary of full employment and a full pay envelope. Without that, it seems to me that all our physical fitness programmes will fail of their effect. If that is not seen to, I am afraid for the success of any programme the government contemplates. We as a nation must find a way to succeed so that we shall never see again a condition in which our citizens are deprived of the means with which to obtain proper food and all the other factors that enter into what constitutes physical fitness.
I bring that to the attention of the minister because I appreciate that no programme, no matter how good it may be on paper, no matter how much the government may wish for its success, can succeed in the future unless the people are able to get the necessary food and to pay for it. They must be able to maintain that standard of living which all of us would like to see them have. But there is another reason why a measure such as this should be introduced. The question of physical fitness suggests the question of relief or the dole, and we all know that the mental very often controls the physical; because men and women who find themselves in conditions that make for despair cannot be physically fit. I therefore make this plea to the government in the hope that in the days ahead of us we shall not only plan for a programme such as that which the minister now envisages in this resolution, but shall make it possible to provide the means whereby such a programme can be properly carried out. Without those means I do not think that success can be attained.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL FOR THE PROMOTION OF PHYSICAL FITNESS
speechtext:
I must congratulate the committee upon the work they have done and the minister upon the services he has rendered the country. In my opinion a -great deal can be done
by way of radio and the opera. A great deal can be done by following the guide which the insurance companies give in the requirements they lay down for their policyholders. There is very little that can be done through the administration of drugs. We shall never revolutionize the world by administering drugs, and I may say that one thing I have always tried to avoid if possible is giving people medicine. The great thing is to give them the proper foods. We should think of drugs as a specialized kind of food which the patient needs at a particular time. Do not draw a line of demarcation between foods and drugs, but give the patient what is necessary for his health, of whatever type it may be, call it drug or food. It can easily be worked out by the doctor in charge.
I like what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) said in regard to finance, but I would point out that the people in this country who have sturdy constitutions are not those who were raised on high finance. There is a saying, blessed is the man who has tasted poverty in his youth. I think that is very true, and I would be sorry to see our young people getting any more money than they have. Instead of raising standards of living, if that means simply giving them more money, we should lower the standards. Think of the people who have died in various towns. The great majority of them have not passed on as a result of Marasmus. Many of them are fellows who could hardly get into their seats; they are the ones who sacrificed themselves on the altars of Bacchus or Vulcan. They are the ones who have disappeared.
The work of the committee should be guided largely by the method of living instead of placing too much emphasis upon giving drugs. If methods of living are guided the nation's health will be greatly benefited.
I appreciate very much the work which the minister is carrying on. We expect great things from this social legislation programme.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL FOR THE PROMOTION OF PHYSICAL FITNESS
speechtext:
For years this group has pointed out the need for some such measure as is introduced by this resolution, and it is greatly to be regretted that a few years ago the nation's health was not deemed worthy of action of this kind. It is disgraceful that there had to be a war to bring out the records of the standards of Canada's health. That health standards were low was generally known, but something prevented action. The excuse that it was a provincial matter and that there were provincial departments of health to look after it is now proved to be an empty one. We cannot but think how much good would
Physical Fitness Act

have been done if in 1930 an expenditure had been undertaken to help Canada in those years of stress.
I am sure the minister will receive with regard to this measure the cooperation which he has asked of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group. What he is proposing is very much in line with the policy we have advocated since the inception of our party. It is to be hoped that this programme will be enlarged, that it is but the beginning of something greater and better. I am sure the minister will find that people throughout the dominion will gladly cooperate with him for the estimable ends at which the resolution aims.
Mr. W. F. IvUHL (Jasper-Edson): Anyone who wishes to see Canada a great nation cannot help but support the principle and the ideas involved in the legislation contemplated by this resolution. It is a self-evident fact that a great nation must be a healthy nation, and I agree entirely with all those who have expressed the sentiment that legislation of this kind is long overdue. But I also agree with, those who have suggested that the question of health is not merely a matter of dealing with the physical deficiencies which exist, but as is the case with all problems which are considered in this house or elsewhere, it resolves itself down in its final essence to where we always arrive at- the question, what are -we to use for money? That is the point I wish to leave with the house in the consideration of this question.
I do not think governments need to point out to individuals the necessity of raising their standard of living and improving their standard of health; these things occur naturally to individuals; and if circumstances are such that they can avail themselves of what is needed to raise their standard of living to what it ought to be, the people will do so. A question which has always arisen before the war is, what are we to use for money? I wish to point out to the house that until every party represented here tackles the question of money, it is idle to talk about solving any problems. When the war is over we shall have a tremendous debt to take care of. The interest on the war debt alone will probably amount to a sum equivalent to what the government was spending for all national services; and if the people are to be expected to pay interest on a debt which I consider is unreal and fictitious and take care of all the other debts which have arisen and endeavour to solve all their problems by means of the monetary policy which was
[Mr. Castleden.l
in vogue prior to the outbreak of war, these problems will be absolutely impossible of solution.
Therefore, on behalf of the Social Credit party, I wish to say that we are not only in sympathy with and have always advocated the highest possible standard of living that was physically possible in this country, but have invariably accompanied our policies with concrete proposals as to how to bring this about. I am not going to enter at the present time into a discussion of monetary policy, but I wish simply to suggest that, unless that problem is tackled, we may as well forget about trying to raise the standard of living and promote health. Solve the money problem, and all other problems will automatically take care of themselves.

Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice):	Mr. Chairman, the hon. member
for Lake Centre had asked me for some information concerning Mrs. Mullins, who had been arrested in St. Joseph de Beauce charged with distributing pamphlets which came under regulation 15A of the defence of Canada regulations because they did not bear the printer's name as required by that regulation, I had promised the hon. member that I would have inquiries made, and I have ascertained that Mrs. Mullins and one Mrs. Boucher were distributing pamphlets and that a member of
War Appropriation-Justice

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at that place reported the matter to the attorney general of Quebec and was instructed by the attorney general of Quebec to procure a search warrant, and having done so, he seized quite a large quantity of these pamphlets bearing no indication of the printer. He thereupon was instructed by the attorney general of Quebec to lay a complaint under regulation 15A, and this was done. The proceedings are under the control of the attorney general of Quebec, as is usual in the administration of justice. These defence of Canada regulations having the force of law are like the provisions of the criminal code in that complaints can be made by any individual. Here the complaint was made on the declaration of the representative of the attorney general of Quebec that this would be handled as an ordinary matter of violation of law. I have not had any subsequent information as to what has been the result of these proceedings. I assume that they are still before the court.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
May I ask whether both parties mentioned by the minister are still in custody?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not know. The information I had was that both had been taken into custody, and when the report was made to me they had not yet been released on bail. I do not know what has taken place since this report.

How long ago were they taken into custody?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The investigation commenced1 on the 2nd of July and the report was sent in on the 9th of July, reporting that a search warrant had been obtained and executed and a charge laid against these two ladies and that they had been apprehended on that charge. The first report was probably made immediately afterwards, but I should not like to be positive as to that. That is the usual procedure. The report bears the date of July 9, 1943.

I cannot allow this item to be passed without some further explanation. This is a serious matter, that a woman under the circumstances disclosed here should have been taken into custody and not given bail on the charges laid against her, of distributing literature not bearing the name and address of the printer according to the provisions of regulation 15A of the defence of Canada regulations, and, second, for being a member of an illegal organization, namely, Jehovah's Witnesses. When people are arrested at a time when we are at war for the

preservation of democratic principles, on the charge of distributing literature that consists of Bible quotations, I feel that something should be done about the matter. If this literature were subversive, I could understand the action taken. But there is no denial of the fact that all that this literature discloses is quotations from the Holy Bible, and the offence charged against these women, for which they may be still in custody and unable to get bail, is that they distributed excerpts from the Bible without having the printer's name endorsed on the pamphlet.

Is that not a matter for the local magistrate? I am only asking. The hon. member may know that it is not. But I think the time of the house should not be occupied with matters of bail if they are within the discretion of the local magistrate.

It is fundamental that the granting of bail rests with the local magistrate. But the administration of the defence of Canada regulations, when the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are used, rests on parliament and the members of this house.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: May I suggest to the hon. member that that is not quite correct. The members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are police constables. The administration of justice throughout Canada is the responsibility of the provincial authorities in the various districts in the provinces, and the sworn police constables have duties which are prescribed by statute. Any individual can lay a charge and the hon. member perhaps knows -I am told from the experience of the department that this is so-that when these persons who call themselves Jehovah's Witnesses are prosecuted, they choose to make martyrs of themselves and go to gaol; they will not ask to be released. They prefer to make their cause notorious by the manner in which they submit to the measures adopted against them. They will not apply for the relief that might be accorded them on appeal.

On the particular facts of this case, does the minister not think a summons would have been the proper course to adopt instead of arresting this person and allowing her to remain in gaol on a charge like this?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That was a matter for the decision of those who were instituting the proceedings. It might be convenient and suit the ideas of a great many people, and it would suit the ideas of a great many who have written to me in connection with this very case, protesting most vigorously, if the ad-

War Appropriation-Justice
ministration of justice were something that was controlled from the Department of Justice and no one else had anything to do with it. But that does not happen to be the British North America Act; and while the British North America Act remains as it is, the Department of Justice cannot have responsibility for the decision of a provincial attorney general or his representative that he will proceed by way of warrant instead of by way of summons.
You would soon get complaints if you tried it.

I want to point out one difficulty in the method of dealing with this item. When the war broke out it was found necessary under the regulations of the War Measures Act to have a committee consider the defence of Canada regulations. Those regulations, after an elaborate study by the present minister's predecessor and his able officials, were considered by a committee of the house. The committee met in the dying days of the first session of the war and agreed upon a long schedule of rules and regulations. Every session the committee has been reconstituted. Last year it met, heard some witnesses and made certain recommendations which have never seen the light of day. Those recommendations of the committee were very important, affecting the liberty of the subject in relation not only to the war but to other matters. For some reason or another they were brought in on the day the house closed, on Friday if I remember rightly, and they have never seen the light of day.
I know a good many Jehovah's Witnesses, not personally, but through letters they have written to me, and I consider that they are perfectly harmless. They believe in religion. I say that when an important committee makes a recommendation the House of Commons has a right to consider it. I hope the Minister of Justice will look into this situation from this point of view. As regards the other regulations, there is a great difference of opinion on the part of the public as to whether they are enforced from a judicial point of view along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre the other day. In some cases these tribunals meet. They meet all over the country, star-chamber tribunals; they report to the minister and announcements are made. I trust that in the recess the minister will review some of these cases and see if some decision cannot be arrived at, so that the public will be informed as to what is going on.

I did not know that this question was coming up or I would have provided myself with the material I intended to use. I wish to say with all the earnestness I possess that the prosecution and persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses under the defence of Canada regulations is a standing disgrace to this country, to the Department of Justice and to the Canadian people. I have on my files a letter reporting an incident that happened in Montreal at a religious meeting where these people gathered for the purpose of performing the rite of holy communion. The place was raided by ten members of the mounted police. The police were asked to wait until after the service, but they would not. They demanded to see the registration cards of those present. There were three women who did not have their registration cards.
Where did this occur?

In the city of Montreal. As I say, three women did not have their registration cards and they were taken to the police station. Suppose the police were to go into any gathering or any church in the evening and ask the congregation to show their registration cards; how many would be found in any congregation of, say, one hundred who would have their cards? Suppose such a thing had happened when the Roman Catholic church was holding a celebration on the streets of Ottawa not so long ago. How we would make the welkin, ring with protests! Any right that is granted to any one religious organization in the country must be granted to all; otherwise we have no religious freedom in Canada. I do not know; I cannot understand, why there should be this continual persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses, because that is what I call it. They may be a nuisance in certain respects, and if they are a nuisance I imagine there is a law to deal with a public nuisance; but it is certainly not the thing to do to declare these people an illegal organization and to use methods such as are being used against them at the present time. I mentioned the other day that the brief presented to the special committee on the defence of Canada regulations last year by the Department of Justice was the weakest thing I had ever seen, seen.
Mr. MaoNICOL:	Pertaining to this
organization?

Yes. There was not enough material in it on which you could shut up a dog, let alone a human being. I would ask the Minister of Justice to present to the house the reasons why this organization is still declared illegal and why it is persecuted by

War Appropriation-Justice
the mounted police. I said at one time that the attitude of the police of any country was a fair indication of the government of that country. For instance, the metropolitan police of London is quite a different body of men from the gestapo of Germany, and the reason is that (the government over the metropolitan police is different from the government in nazi Germany. So that we shall get from the police exactly what the government intends that we should get from them.

Can the hon. gentleman say after the dinner recess how many Jehovah's Witnesses there are in the country and how many young men of military age have been exempted on account of their conscientious objection?

I have no intention of saying anything of the kind. It has nothing to do with the discussion. It is not germane to it.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I should like to ask the minister a question with reference to what was said this afternoon. I do not know anything about the sect called Jehovah's Witnesses, but I was greatly interested in and amazed at what the hon. member for Lake Centre told the committee, and I would ask the minister if it is the fact that anyone distributing religious pamphlets anywhere in any province can be arrested if the name of the printer is not on the pamphlet. I know nothing about the law as to whether the name of the printer should be on a pamphlet, except that it must be on political pamphlets distributed during an election. I was very much amazed also at what the hon. member for Vancouver East said, when he told about some meeting of these people, at which a religious service was going on, being interrupted by members of the mounted police, who apparently went rather rudely through the meeting taking names and asking those present if they had registration cards with them. I did not know that things like that went on in Canada. I know some folks in my part of Toronto who belong to this sect, and, while I know nothing of the sect itself, I have always recognized them as decent, law-abiding people. I have not heard of any of them committing any offence, and I would be much surprised if they did. So that I feel that in this day, with the sun shining
l Mr. Maclnnis.]
above, and a clear blue sky and stars at night, we have got to a line pass if people cannot worship as they see fit.
I remember that the last time I was in Scotland I went to the Greyfriars church in Edinburgh to see the spot where my ancestors cut their veins, with others who attended there, and either put a quill or a pen into their veins and signed the Solemn League and Covenant. They, too, were being persecuted in Scotland in those days-I have forgotten by whom, and it does not matter- but they would not stand for it. Nor would I stand for any persecution. I have no fault to find with anyone's religious belief or how he worships. That is none of my business. People can stand on their heads or stand in a corner if they wish; I do not care what they do. I had hoped the time had arrived when people could worship as they liked without any interference. I did not know that anywhere in Canada such things were going on as were reported here this afternoon.
I ask the minister if it is true, as the hon. member for Lake Centre says, that people can be arrested for distributing any kind of religious tract because it does not bear the name of the printer. I should also like to know whether, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has said, a religious service in Montreal was interfered with, and rather rudely so, by the mounted police.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think the hon. member was not here when these matters were being considered on a previous occasion. I gave then some of the information which had been given to me with reference to this sect of Jehovah's Witnesses; it is recorded in Hansard and I do not think I need repeat it.
With respect to the questions the hon. member has put. First of all, as to the application of defence of Canada regulation 15A, it provides that:
Every printed newspaper, pamphlet, circular, handbill, dodger, or other like document having reference to or containing any comment on a political, social or religious question, shall bear upon it printed in a conspicuous place and in legible characters the name of an existing natural person. . . .
Now, as to whether that would apply to the kind of material that was being distributed in St. George de Beauce, of course I am not in a position to express any opinion. I believe the hon. member for Lake Centre said that he had a copy of some of the material which was distributed. I am quite sure that this regulation, in the manner in which it is drawn, -would not apply to a sheet which would

War Appropriation-Justice
contain nothing more than extracts from the bible; that would not be something which would be within the definition of this article. I thank the hon. member for Lake Centre for having sent over this document. I will not take time to examine it now, and even if I didi I would not venture to express here an opinion upon a matter which is at present before the courts. But the regulation as it is exposes anyone who violates it to be proceeded against.
With respect to the second question, there was some report in the newspapers at the time and the matter was carefully investigated. It was found that a meeting was being held, but what kind of meeting was not known to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They went there and requested the persons in attendance to exhibit their registration cards. That is something which is provided for by the national registration regulations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
May I ask at how many meetings in that city a similar request was made by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not know.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does the minister know
of any other case?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Where requests
were made to people attending a gathering?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Oh, yes. I cannot
speak of Montreal, but I know that in my own city of Quebec there have been such cases. At a meeting some time ago the police attended and asked to check the registration cards. At that time, some months ago, the contention was being made that quite a number of people had not registered. That arose out of the fact that call-ups were being made; apparently quite a number of people in the age groups subject to the proclamation were going about their ordinary occupations without having received any call-up, and an effort was made to see whether the registration regulations had been carried out.
With respect to this meeting, I was informed that at the time the police did not know what kind of meeting it was. As regards the defence of Canada regulations which were passed at the outbreak of war, and particularly in respect of this banning of a certain number of organizations which was made in 1940, there was an amendment passed in February, 1943, in which it was declared that it would not be an offence to attend any meeting the purpose
of which was religious worship or instruction. Perhaps I had better give the exact language which was inserted in the regulations:
No person shall be guilty of an offence against this regulation by reason only of his attending a meeting the sole purpose of which is religious worship or instruction.
As the regulation was previously drawn, it could very well be argued that, with respect to Technocrats, the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, Incorporated, the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, the International Bible Students' Society, and Jehovah's Witnesses, the very fact of attending one of their gatherings where they worship in the form which they think is the proper form would be an offence. So that I recommended and had an amendment made that it would not be an offence for members of these banned organizations to attend the meetings for purposes of religious worship or instruction.
The information I got was that this request for registration cards was made by the police in an orderly fashion and that nothing was done there which would not have been done at any other meeting where an attempt was made to see if those attending it were provided with their national registration certificates.
Mr. MacNI'COL: Were those at that meeting who did not happen to have their registration cards with them arrested and taken away?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not know what was done, in fact, but they would be liable to be dealt with in that way, just as any member of this house would.

I carry mine with me.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have mine, too. That is the.provision; whether or not it be a wise provision-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is quite a testimonial meeting in itself.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: -it is provided by the regulations that one can be stopped by a peace officer at any time, anywhere, and asked to show his registration card.

I believe in regulations being adhered to.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is the regulation. At the time it was made it was necessary. Whether or not it is still necessary may be a matter upon which opinions may vary, but it is still the regulation. With respect to the activities of these Jehovah's Witnesses, the other day I stated that tens of millions of their tracts and pamphlets have been put out from their Watch Tower head office in New
War Appropriation-Justice

York. Their teaching is that all these organized religions are agencies of the devil. They do not call their sect a religion, but they believe the organized religions are agencies to maintain the devil's embrace on the human race. They understand from the bible that it is wrong to go to war, and they are conscientious objectors.

They do not vote, either, dio they?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	I do not know
whether they vote, but they will not salute the flag; that, according to them, is an act of idolatry. At the present time-and the same situation is still continuing-they are detrimental to the war morale of this nation. Only this morning the commissioner received a report of a complaint made by Mr. Justice Embury in Regina about the activities of the Jehovah's Witnesses there, who are persuading the young men to go before the boards and claim exemption on the ground that they should not fight because it is wrong and contrary to the teachings of the bible. A declaration at this time which would be construed by them and by the public as a recognition of their legality by this parliament would, in my opinion, be detrimental to the morale of this country.
The administration of the regulations, as I said this afternoon, like the administration of the criminal law can be set in motion by the attorneys-general of the several provinces of Canada, and the Department of Justice cannot hold itself responsible for the form of procedure adopted in the respective provinces. What this parliament could do; what the government of Canada could do, would be to repeal these provisions, and then the provincial authorities could not proceed upon them. But while the provisions are there, we cannot be held responsible for the manner in which the provincial authorities proceed upon them.
After the committee rose for the dinner recess I had the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police communicate with the authorities who had directed the institution of these proceedings against Mrs. Mullins. The information now given me is that she was arrested on the 8th of July; was offered bail on the 9th and refused; was released on her personal recognizance without bail on the 19th, because there was a further adjournment to the 26th for the hearing of her case. The further information was given the commissioner that, as he understood it, the attorney-general was going to file a nolle prosequi on the 26th. That I do not know, but it might very well result from the fact, if it is a fact,

that this pamphlet contains nothing but extracts from the 'Crampon version of the Bible, which is one of the reputed French versions authorized by the Roman Catholic church. It is the one upon which I took my oath of office before his excellency and upon which I took my oath of office before the Clerk of this house, which volumes were fittingly inscribed and which I intend to hand down as precious documents to the members of my family. It may very well be that when the attorney-general saw that there was nothing but extracts from the Crampon version of the Bible he came to the conclusion that his representations had been too hasty. That I cannot affirm; I have not verified that with the authorities themselves, but this is the information the commissioner obtained over the long-distance telephone during the dinner recess.
I understand there was also a charge laid against Mrs. Mullins of being a member of the sect of Jehovah's Witnesses. That is no longer an offence; the sect is banned. At the same time that this other amendment was made I caused this regulation to be amended, because I pointed out that these organizations having been declared illegal, they could not do anything that would have any legal effect; and if before the banning one was a member thereof, there was no way in which he could have legal effect given to his desire to withdraw and cease to be a member. So that the regulation was amended to provide that instead of its being an offence to belong to one of these banned organizations, it would be an offence to act as an officer or member thereof.

What is the number of that order in council?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: P,C. 1266, of February 15, 1943.

Would the minister be good enough to read it?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Previously the regulation read:
Every person who is an officer or member of an illegal organization, or professes to be such, or who advocates or defends the acts, principles or policies of such illegal organization shall be guilty of an offence against this regulation.
The amendment changed that to read:
Every person who acts as an officer or member of an illegal organization or who advocates or defends the acts, principles or policies of such illegal organization shall be guilty of an offence against this regulation.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni will note that we were amending in line with his argument of the other day that intentions should not make one a criminal, that there ought to be acts manifesting participation.

War Appropriation-Justice

Would the minister also give the order in council in regard to having the name printed on documents?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am sorry I cannot give at this moment the original order in council, because it was included in the consolidation of 1942 and is now in existence by virtue of P.C. 8862 of October 13, 1942, but it had been enacted prior to that. I shall get it for the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, the last
time the minister's estimates were before the committee I pointed out that under the defence of Canada regulations he had the power to defend the people of this country . from the machinations of the enemy, but that so far as I could see he had in some instances failed to perform his duty. I refer to section 39A of the defence of Canada regulations which states:
No person shall print, make, publish, issue, have knowingly in his possession in quantity, circulate or distribute any book, newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture, paper, circular, card, letter, writing, print, publication or document of any kind containing any material, report or statement,
(a) intended or likely to cause disaffection to His Majesty or to interfere with the success of His Majesty's forces or of the forces of any allied or associated powers, or to prejudice His Majesty's relations with foreign powers.
And this is the part I wish to emphasize: ... or to prejudice His Majesty's relations with foreign powers.
A while ago, in one of his great speeches the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Winston Churchill, said:
Whoever by word of mouth or by written statement attempt to destroy the unity of the united nations, it were better for him that a millstone were hung about his neck, and he were cast into the sea.
From time to time we have had in Canada publications, newspapers, which have published material, articles and statements which,
I submit, to the minister, would contravene paragraph (a) of section 39A of the regulations in that they prejudice his majesty's relations with foreign powers.
I would refer the minister particularly to several of the editorials which have appeared from time to time in the Evening Telegram of Toronto. I refer specifically to an item published on July 17, a reprint from the Reader's Digest, and headed, "To collaborate successfully we must face the facts about Russia." It is an article by a writer named Max Eastman, and contains the type of material which, in my opinion, will be most difficult for Mr. Wilgress to explain in Moscow.
I feel that the relationships between our two
nations at present will not stand discriminatory articles of this type, and if the minister were doing his duty he would, under the defence of Canada regulations, prosecute those who fill the minds of the people with trash such as this article undoubtedly is. It contains under one caption a statement which is known to be a direct forgery made by a fascist, and put into the mouth of Mr. Stalin.
I have mentioned the fact that this article is a reprint taken from the Readers' Digest, and printed in the Evening Telegram. There are, no doubt, many people who have a very good opinion of the Reader's Digest. But perhaps it would be just as well to state one or two facts concerning this publication, facts which might not be known to everybody. In the United States right after Pearl Harbor one of the first magazines which was stopped by the United States government from further publication was Scribners' Commentator. This was a magazine which was not allowed to be published any more, on the ground that it was one of the leading fascist publications. It favoured Franco, Hitler and Japan. Its editor was George Egglestone. George Egglestone to-day is a writer for the Reader's Digest. He had an associate editor whose name was Ralph Townsend, who is now in the penitentiary, because he was found to be a Japanese propaganda agent.

It is important that we should remember this when we hear German propaganda, which is working artfully in your country and in mine, and all over the world, whispering lies, in their effort to split Russia away from the Englishspeaking world, and the united nations, and to divorce and destroy the confidence of the English-speaking world in the integrity and good faith of our great Russian ally. I do not rise at this time to quarrel with the Minister of Justice or to enter into a religious controversy. It has. been my experience for a good many years that whenever you want to divide the people,, to separate and disunite them on any subject or for any purpose, the quickest way to do so is to introduce this question of religion. It has been used for a good many years for that purpose. I say I do not rise to quarrel with the Minister of Justice, because I d*o not consider that the present minister is responsible for the regulations which he has had to defend since coming into this house, and my opinion is that the defence of Canada regulations committee, which was appointed by the house and sat during the last session to consider the regulations and their amendments, fell down on the job. I am not accusing any member of the committee or relieving anyone of his share of the responsibility, because if that committee sat in camera, and deliberated upon this matter for months, bringing their deliberations to a finality in a report, then it was the responsibility of the committee to bring that report to the house and to see that the members of the house were given an opportunity to vote on it. That was not

War Appropriation-Justice
done. I agree with the minister when he says that, as far as the making of the laws is concerned, that is the job of the House of Commons, and to ask him to lift the ban on anything or to change the regulations is to give him a power to which he is not entitled. That is the job of the House of Commons. The regulations were passed by order in council. I do not agree with them, and I am not asking the minister now to take power with which I do not agree. I am laying the responsibility for the ban not being lifted at the doors of the defence of Canada regulations committee.
I believe the time has come for a reexamination of the regulations on this particular question. In 1939, when the regulations were brought out, we had an entirely different situation. The country was going to war. The country was wholly disorganized from the viewpoint of preparation for war. Nobody knew who anybody was; the regulations were laid down as an emergency act, and everyone who might come under suspicion was included in them. That went on until last year, and I think the committee then, with a cooling of the hysteria which existed at the time the regulations were passed, was in a position to survey the whole matter calmly and make specific recommendations to the house. That was not done; the committee shirked its responsibility. I suggest that adoption of the committee's report, which was tabled at the last session, should be moved before this house rises, because when a House of Commons committee comes to a decision based on the views of the majority it should be brought before this house, hon. members given an opportunity of voting on it, and the recommendations implemented.
I am concerned in this matter about one thing, the loss of liberty of any section of our people, because if you follow the growth of nazism; if you examine the history of the rise of Hitler and Mussolini to power, you will find that they did not try to take the people's liberties away all at once; they manoeuvred around; they banned the "tin-hats" and youth clubs in Germany; they limited the powers and gradually destroyed the functions of Rotary clubs and similar organizations, until finally they could set up the full machinery of dictatorship. Having watched the growth of nazism in Europe, I am convinced that unless the people in any country fully understand that they must not allow the liberties of any section of the population to be taken from them, it will be only a matter of time until our turn comes. It is the thin end of the wedge. I do not say that anyone on the 72537-3291
defence of Canada regulations committee or in the Department of Justice has any intention of travelling that road, but I am not so sure that there are not other people in this country who would1 travel it were they given the opportunity.
On this matter of Jehovah's Witnesses, I know many of these people in my own end of the country. I have some as friends and neighbours, and I know they are the best citizens in the community. They practise the brotherhood of man; their creed is " Love thy neighbour as thyself"; they accept their full share of responsibilities; they pay their bills. The only accusation I ever heard against them' was that they make a nuisance of themselves;: they pass around a lot of literature; they want to sell you a book every afternoon, and that kind of stuff. But we have freedom in this country to do that sort of thing; I am free to tell that fellow to get away from the door if I do not want to talk to him. I believe that to ban them as a subversive element, or an element causing dissatisfaction in his majesty's forces, or as in any way interfering with the war effort, is ridiculous, and it was an absolute mistake to include them under the defence of Canada regulations. Many of the people in question who are convinced that this is the kind of religion they should practise have sons and daughters in the armed forces. I know some of them personally; they are making their contribution. If the father or mother thinks this is the way in which they should worship God1, I believe they should be given the opportunity. According to the Ottawa Citizen of recent date, if General Eisenhower's-mother were living in this country she would' be under this ban; she is a member of this group. In the United States they have not gone to the extent that we have in Canada in measures against this sect. I believe something was done in a restrictive way, but the courts of the United States gave them considerably more freedom than they have in Canada. The same applies to Australia, where the issue was exactly the same as we have it, and to-day they are as free there to earry on as is any other religious group.
I am not quarrelling with the Minister of Justice. He inherited the defence of Canada regulations. When they were drafted the situation was entirely different. Naturally there was a general weeding-out process gone through, but I think that on the basis of conditions to-day the minister would be well advised to review the whole matter, and if he-has any supervision or jurisdiction over the defence of Canada regulations committee, he
War Appropriation-Justice

should instruct them to complete the work they started last session by moving the report in the house, which would eliminate this issue now and in the future.

That is a very proper question. I think the proceedings might be commenced, where an offence is believed to have been committed, by the police authorities or by the agencies for the prosecution of offences in the various provinces, but the continuation of these prosecutions should be determined by the Attorney General of Canada. I think that is the only way in which it will be ensured that injustice such as occurred to Mrs. Mullins shall not be permitted. It is a serious matter to place a person in the position in which she was placed, having committed no offence but being held in custody. There is no way in which she can be recompensed; there is no provision for that. For all time there will be a suggestion that she did something contrary to the safety of the state in time of war, which is a serious matter. As far as possible that sort of thing should be guarded against.

Perhaps the real point at issue in this discussion is becoming obscured. I do not imagine that any hon. member would desire to suggest that under the regulations, either by action of the minister or of the mounted police, anyone in this country should be prosecuted, much less arrested, for entertaining a religious belief. We are all past that stage. Such things were done two hundred years ago in the name of religion by enthusiasts who failed to appreciate the Sermon on the Mount, who thought the proper punishment for those who disagreed with their particular religious belief was to burn them at the stake as heretics. I imagine no one would suggest that we in Canada would tolerate any prosecution or persecution, as it has been called, on such grounds. But I wish to point out to the committee and particularly to those hon. members who perhaps feel strongly and who have spoken during this discussion this evening, that nothing in the defence of Canada regulations tolerates the arrest or persecution of any man or woman for a religious belief. I must

War Appropriation-Justice
quarrel with the hon. member who is leading the Social Credit party for the moment, the hon. member for Macleod, who says he endorses the theory that we object to, as put forward by Jehovah's Witnesses, when they declared in Canada in 1941 and 1942 that human laws are not binding upon them if, in their opinion, those human laws, which are the laws of Canada, conflict with their view of divine law.
Is that not so in peace time as well?

Certainly ; but I think when my hon. friend reflects upon his assent to that proposition he will desire to inform the house some day soon that he did not mean it. What is he preaching, or what doctrine is he endorsing? He is a British subject, a Canadian; and under the British practice parliament decides the laws that shall govern British subjects. The doctrine of these people which he has just endorsed-and I hope he will soon repent, for I suspect that at times he preaches repentance-is that in their view the law which the parliament of Canada has put upon the statute books to govern the conduct of our citizens, either within or without the criminal law, means nothing to them; that they will defy it, disregard it and break it if it does not conform to their conception of divine law. Well, Mr. Chairman, that is awfully close, let me warn the hon. member, to preaching subversive doctrines either in peace time or in war.
What is his remedy? When these people put that doctrine into effect; when they break the criminal law of Canada and defy the laws that, parliament has enacted, he blandly says to our overworked Minister of Justice, Well, just arrest them, because beyond arresting them the state is not concerned with the preaching of that kind of subversive doctrine, particularly in war time. In the committee on the defence of Canada regulations, of which I had the honour to be a member, hon. gentlemen will recall that it was shown that these people held meetings under the guise of propagating and preaching their particular religious doctrine. The amendment which, I am sure in his wisdom, has been made by the minister lessening the severity of their having been banned, takes care of that sort of thing and permits them to hold their religious meetings. As long as they confine themselves to their doctrine or religion, there can be no interference, because they are protected.
I think some hon. members who have spoken to-night have failed to appreciate that the preaching of a religious doctrine is one
thing and advising young men in Canada to refuse to serve their country in this time of war is another thing. We met here for five days in September, 1939. We had no chance to consult our constituents; we did not need to. With two or three exceptions the members of this parliament declared that Canada would stand by the side of the mother country in this war. We did so, not from any compulsion because when Great Britain is at war Canada is at war. That old theory was exploded. We came here and said, on behalf of the people of Canada, "When the mother country is at war we seek and propose to stand by her side, and to send our men to help her." It was said-and I think it has been shown to have been correctly said-that the British channel is probably the last line of defence for Canada. And we sent, and are proud to have sent, our young men overseas to the extent of hundreds of thousands, in the three armed forces.
There has been a good deal of heat put on in this debate. An attack has been made upon the Boyal Canadian Mounted Police, than which thene is no finer force in all the world. There has also been an attack upon our Minister of Justice, who I believe is endeavouring to do the best possible job. I pay tribute to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, with whom I seldom agree, for his ready acquiescence in a refusal- although some of his colleagues did not see the light-to pour condemnation on our Minister of Justice for performing a very difficult task in war time.
But let me just point this out, that the subversive teachings of Jehovah's Witnesses to the youth of Canada were in direct opposition to the request of the government of Canada to the young men of this country to carry out the declared war policy of Canada, and to enlist in the three services for service anywhere in the world. They were invited so to do. The Jehovah's Witnesses said, "No; you should not do it"; and they preached their religious doctrine in support of a subversive policy, in direct conflict with the lavv of this country laid down by a unanimous parliament.
But they are not the only people in this country who laid down a doctrine, as they had a right to do, a policy which was in direct contradiction of the policy this government enacted. The Cooperative Commonwealth party, among whom I hope I have some personal friends, placed upon Hansard on the 9th day of September, 1939, a solemn declaration of their attitude toward military participation in this war, and they did not
