do so lightly. The hon. member for Rose to wn-Biggar made this clear, and for the benefit of hon. members I may say it is to be found at page 55 of Hansard of that famous wartime session:	.
May I say that this is the policy, not only of the majority of our parliamentary group, but of our national council which met for two days this week and which represents the consensus of the leaders of our movement from coast to coast. I propose to place this policy upon the records of the house so that parliament and the country may have a clear idea of what it means. Our statement of policy reads . . .
I shall not trouble the committee with those paragraphs which do not deal directly with the topic under discussion at this time. However, item No. 3 says:
No military participation overseas.
That is the declared1 policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation at a session when Great Britain's back was against the wall, in September, 1939!
IMr. HANSELL: May I ask the minister-
Borne hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

-or the hon. member- perhaps he will aspire to being a minister some day-whether or not he would recommend the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation being declared a subversive institution, and therefore banned?

Certainly not, and my hon. friend well knows why. Let me say to him, in parenthesis, that his party, through my good friend, the hon. member for Lethbridge, made a sound and magnificent patriotic declaration that they would have no part of a weakling policy of no participation overseas, and he made it clear. I refer to this matter this evening, not to chide my hon. friends in any improper way, but to point out that if they were to be entrusted with the government of this country, I would ask the people of Canada first to consider whether, with the empire in a crisis, their declared policy, properly placed upon the records of parliament, was a policy that they are not now fully ashamed of.
They are loyal people in this way; they believe in parliamentary institutions and in declaring their policy before parliament. They did not come out after that declaration of their policy was outvoted and re-declare the policy . of not standing by the side of the mother country and participating in the fighting overseas. If they had thereafter gone out and preached this kind of doctrine, I am not at all sure, may I say to my hon. friends, that they would not have been in the class that declares that parliament does not matter, if the law of

God does not carry their mind to carry out the law of Canada. They did not do any such thing, and I do not accuse them of any such thing.
Just another word with regard to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, with whom to-night I was in practically full accord. I think he took a stand which did his party credit, and I am sorry the other hon. member I am looking at did not take a similar stand, when he wanted to pick and hack at the Minister of Justice. But I do have a little quarrel with the hon. member for Cape Breton South, because it may be recalled that in Hamilton, in March of this year, under the auspices of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, at a Sunday afternoon meeting in a theatre he addressed a group of labour men, and made a statement-and I think it was a pity, because we were still recruiting, and we are recruiting to-day. This statement was not made under the protection of parliament. It was made, I am afraid as a rabble-rousing effort at a Sunday afternoon labour meeting, under the auspices of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. This is what he said, as it was reported in the Hamilton Spectator, and I put it on Hansard and ask him to deny it. I will read his language. This is what he said on that Sunday afternoon:
The people will have to get rid of the Churchills to attain their ideals.
March, 1943! Great Britain still in dire need! A God-given leader in Winston Churchill, whom a gentleman had no right to criticize! And he says to his Cooperative Commonwealth Federation comrades in Hamilton, "The people will have to get rid of the Churchills to attain their ideals"! Well, that may be the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation ideal, but I do not think you can get any other member, including the hon. member for North Battleford, to abuse Winston Churchill. That hon. member is British, I think. She is proud of Winston Churchill, as we are, all of us, proud of him. And when I charged him with that statement, and challenged him to deny it-and I hoped he might have said he was misreported-what did he say? On April 6, as it appears at page 1914 of Hansard, he said:
I have no intention of denying it, and under the proper item I shall reiterate and explain it to the satisfaction of the hon. member.
Well, as far as I can recall, that "proper item" has not come along. He has not dared to reiterate it, nor has he attempted to explain it.
Where does that leave him and his party? He did not go to Hamilton by accident. He

War Appropriation-Justice
went to Hamilton on the invitation of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in Ontario. And I have not heard any of the leaders of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in Ontario repudiate that statement. I want to leave in the judgment of this committee whether that condemnation is a slur, a besmirching of Winston Churchill, the hon. member's daring to say to the people of Canada-let me get it exactly right 

"the people will have to get rid of the Churchills to attain their ideals." What are the ideals that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation entertain which necessitate ridding the empire of Winston Churchill? The hon. member has a full chance to reiterate and I should like to hear him explain it. He is advertised somewhere in Ontario, I believe in a campaign that is said to be going on there; I believe there is said to be a campaign in Ontario-
You can tell that when you are speaking to-night.

-as being a man of great boldness in the House of Commons. If that is boldness, God forbid that we teach young Canadians to be bold.
Mr. MaeINNIS: You do not need to cast any slurs upon the hon. member for Cape Breton South for lack of boldness.

I am quoting an advertisement which was paid for by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in the province of Ontario. It is not my language; I would not call him bold.
Mr. MaeINNIS: What is wrong with that?

Nothing wrong with it.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Why are you taking up time with it?

Do you not like it?
Mr. MaeINNIS:	Oh, yes.

My hon. friend for whom
I have a high regard has challenged me and said that I am taking up time with this. I will ask him a simple question and I will sit down while he answers it. Will he dare to say to this committee that the people will have to get rid of the Churchills to attain their ideals?
Mr. MaeINNIS: That is not the question.

All right, I will go on. I
rose to point out that we have been under a misapprehension, and my hon. friends across the floor have been under a genuine misapprehension. They are perfectly right to come
forward and champion the cause of religion and the right of every man to engage in the religion he likes. But this country is at war, and when you are at war and you use religion as a cloak to urge the youth of Canada to disobey and defy the laws of Canada, then I say that your divine law should not spare you.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Mr. Chairman we have heard a typical lawyer's speech. Not having anything to advance against the arguments which were made from this side of the house urging that the persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses be stopped, the hon. member talked about something else. Any good lawyer can do that; every good lawyer always does it when he has not a case. That is the way in which he makes his living. He said that these people were using their religion as a cloak to do things that were detrimental to the war. The hon. member no doubt knows there are sections in the defence of Canada regulations which take care of actions of that kind without having to put a whole religious organization under a ban of illegality, without having to invade churches where people are partaking [DOT] of holy communion, without having to interrupt their service to ask for registration cards, without having to take people off to the police station because they have not their card. Let me tell my hon. friend that he does not need to look over here for either obstruction or objection to Canada's war effort. If my hon. friend will only look behind, he will see plenty of it.
On every possible occasion reference is made to the attitude of this party. We did take that attitude, but we were compelled to take it on account of the attitude that my hon. friend and his friends took in the years preceding the war. You supplied the enemy with the means of war; you assisted Hitler and Mussolini during the years between 1936 and 1939 to destroy democracy in every part of Europe. How did we know that you were not going to do the same thing again? The people of Britain had to do the same thing; they had to get rid of certain leaders before they could get on with the war As the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) said the other day, it was considered a phoney war until the fall of France. When we arrived here in May, 1940, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) said that they, the government, could not get on with production because they could not get the requisite plans and processes from Great Britain. British industrialists had decided to make it a capitalist war, as is being done here.
War Appropriation-Justice

But that has nothing to do with the question at issue, the question of Jehovah's Witnesses being declared an illegal organization. Why have they been declared an illegal organization in the first place? I submit that the Minister of Justice has not yet put on record a clear statement that would 'be satisfactory to this committee as to why that was done. My hon. friend has not done that. The special committee on the defence of Canada regulations which met last year heard all the evidence that the Department of Justice brought before it; it heard all the witnesses for the defence of Canada regulations, and as far as my memory goes the committee was unanimous in recommending that the ban on the Jehovah's Witnesses should be raised. My hon. friend was a member of that committee. Why did he not rise in the committee and face those Jehovah's Witnesses? He could not face them with the argument he made here to-night, because that argument was not applicable in the committee. He had to meet them with the facts, but he did not meet them with the facts. But this fact still remains; that is, that no evidence has been placed before this committee that would justify the declaring of the Jehovah's Witnesses an illegal organization. In my opinion it is clear, pure religious prejudice that is maintaining the ban.

I do not want to continue this discussion, but I -have been anxious to have something to say about the old age pension system that we have. I must confess that I think that the Communists and Jehovah's Witnesses are getting altogether too much attention as -compared with what attention we are giving to our old age- pensioners. I just want to say this to the committee-
Old age pensions have nothing to do with this matter.

I am not talking about old age pensions. I got past that before you decided it was out of order. I am speaking about this particular matter. I wish to say to the Minister of Justice that surely the time has come when we should have a set of rules and regulations in this house under which the things that should be debated can be debated and useless debate of the kind we have had to-night not be permitted to take up the time of parliament as has been done.
So far as I am concerned, and I hold just as strong convictions as anyone in -this committee, I think it is a mistake to have a ban on communism, and I think it is a mistake to have a ban on Jehovah's Witnesses. I believe the best security against these kinds of isms
[Mr. Maclnnis.3
is to let them come out and expose themselves. I believe we can depend upon the patriotism and common sense of the people of Canada to take care of themselves. But when parliament has made a decision that is an expression of the overwhelming majority of this house, it does seem to me to be an obvious waste of time to repeat over and over again arguments that the overwhelming majority of this house have repudiated, and repudiated with, I believe, the overwhelming support of the people of the Dominion of Canada. Surely the day has come when we can transact the business of Candda along something like the same lines of orderly procedure that is followed in the British House of Commons, and surely this debate to-night is clear evidence of the need of bringing up to date the rules governing debate in this house.

I am not rising now to answer the hon, member for Parry Sound. As far as what he has said about me is concerned, I am quite willing to let my record stand not only as a patriotic citizen of Canada but also as a law-abiding citizen. I think that when his speech is analysed to-morrow it will not appear so sound as it sounded to-night.
I rise just to ask one question of the minister. It is a simple question. These people known as Jehovah's Witnesses are frightened to assemble themselves together. I wish they could be relieved of that fear and that, some publicity could be given to the regulation which permits them to gather together in worship.
There is one other matter. I have said that they were frightened. I have had, over the past year and in the past few days particularly, no end of letters which have been sent unsigned, anonymous letters from these people, and the reason why they are sent anonymously is that these people are frightened to sign their names. Some of them say so. I am not bringing this up because it is an important matter but on account of the principle involved. Why should people be frightened by any regulations? I wish to ask the minister, will he just assure these people that they can write to members of parliament and to their friends on these matters, and sign their names without any fear of coming under the defence of Canada regulations. That is a simple request, and I believe that the minister should assure these people of at least some protection in that respect.
I should like an answer from the minister.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I can give no other assurance than that which is provided by the text of the regulations which were published at the time in the Canada Gazette. If that is

War Appropriation-Justice
not enough for them, I do not know that there is anything more that I can accord to them.
The minister will not even say that they can write a letter and sign their name?

I should like to make a few comments on certain things the hon. member for Parry Sound said to-night. If the arguments he put forward are logical, I think we might well ask this question: Why is it that the government has not long since placed the ban upon the Doukhobors? I was in British Columbia two years ago, and while I was there the Doukhobors burned down a packing plant because they wanted to force the fruit growers in that community to sell their fruit through their organization. The growers got together and built another building. Before it was completed, it, too, was burned down. While there was not absolute proof that the Doukhobors burned it down, that was the general belief throughout the district, and the provincial police with whom I spoke at the time admitted that the Doukhobors had burned down the building.
I was also told that forest fires which were continually occurring around the district were set by the Doukhobors in order that they would be able to get a job fighting the fire. That kind of action was subversive. I think the Doukhobors have not been prominent in their support of the war effort. Sometimes I become convinced of the fact that this action regarding Jehovah's Witnesses is largely a religious question. Some three years ago a couple of men called at my house on the prairie one morning. I did not know who they were. They asked me whether they could play a couple of records. I thought at first they were salesmen for a certain make of phonograph. We gave them permission to put on the records and they played them. They were two recordings of the man by the name of Judge Rutherford. I want to give the committee the assurance that in those two speeches by Judge Rutherford there was not one word of a subversive nature. The whole of the two speeches was a bitter attack on the Roman Catholics. I do not suppose that is considered subversive. It is intolerable, I will admit. I do not approve that type of attack. But it does make one wonder whether the action against Jehovah's Witnesses is largely on account of their attitude toward the Roman Catholics, instead of their attitude of a subversive nature.
Mr. LaFLECHE: That is a shame.
You may say that it is a shame, but that question is being asked all over this country. I am asked it from one end of Canada to the other, and I am just repeating the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I was not aware that my hon. friend had travelled all over Canada from one end to the other.
I have travelled over many parts of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I can say this and I have some knowledge whereof I speak. There is not a single particle of evidence to support the allegation which the hon. member made in his concluding remarks.
I did not make any allegation. I asked a question that is being asked all over the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: It was close to an allegation, if it was not an allegation. I think all members will agree on reflection that it is a most unwise sort of statement to make. He raised the question whether the policy of the government so far as Jehovah's Witnesses was concerned was inspired by their attack on the Roman Catholic church. That is the only inference that could be drawn from his statement. I wish to say that that inference has no foundation whatsoever, and I want that to go across this country. The raising of issues of this kind, the planting of seeds of doubt and suspicion is the greatest disservice that can be rendered to Canada at the present time.

The suspicion is there. I am not planting it.
Mr. CPlERAR: I repudiate absolutely the implication in the remarks of the hon. member.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police-[DOT]
Increased activities of the force due to the war, $6,091,320.

In mentioning the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I do so merely because I have had some slight connection with them during the present war. Prior to the war the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were a small but efficient technical force. They had come down from the old Royal Northwest Mounted Police who wore the red coat and rode the horse, the days when the red coat and the horse were symbols of British justice in the great territories of the northwest. Through science they became an efficient and almost international police force whose name was known from one corner of the world to the other. In the beginning of the war there was no force that received such small recognition as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in the matter of pay. Their pay at that time was even less than the pay of the private soldier in the Canadian army. They were subject to various restrictions with regard to marriage and freedom in one way or another, and a protest was raised in this house.
The first thing that happened was that they did receive an increase in pay, and first of all, let me say that I consider that increase inadequate, having regard to the work which the force has done. It is a small, highly-trained, extremely efficient force, and the money we expend on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is one of the best investments we have ever made in this house.
It is not luck that we have had no sabotage in Canada. It is not luck that we have not had mysterious fires. It is not luck that we have not had a number of enemy agents loose. Further, it is not luck that there has been so little sabotage in the United States. I merely mention that we were at war for a long period before the United States became a belligerent; and when the history of this war is written, as I hope it will be written some day, and the place of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is properly evaluated, we shall have, I believe, cause to appreciate what this force has done for Canada.
I make these observations now because there are two objections I have to the present set-up of the force. The first objection is

that the force, with the present pay and allowances, is a far lower basic rate than the federal bureau of investigation. I think they are doing equally important work as that done by the F.B.I., and the first point I want to bring out is that this force should be paid on the same basic rates as the F.B.I. Equal pay for equal work is an axiom of democracy. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are doing equally important work with the federal bureau of investigation, technical work that requires the highest possible efficiency and training, work that cannot be learned or understood until men have had years of training. They are doing that work and in my opinion are not receiving adequate recompense for it.
The second point on which I disagree with the policy is this. The functions of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have altered. In the old days in the northwest territories, when the red coat meant his majesty's justice, that red coat was a symbol, and it was an efficient symbol that justice would be done throughout the length and breadth of this great land. The red coats of the mounted police have, however, been used to an extent which I think is questionable as a show or a parade ground force. These men are too valuable to be used merely as guards and as a show force. They have received training, sometimes going into many areas, and I think their use as guards is undesirable. I am not speaking of the temporary constables with the armband who serve as guards in our public buildings, but I object to -the use of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as guards of dominion public buildings. Their job is far higher and more important than merely that of custodians of public property. I wish I could say what their job has been during the war, but it has been so important that I should like to see the use of the words "Royal Canadian Mounted Police" divorced from the mere guarding of buildings, from the man who stands in the corridor and takes your pass. In my opinion he is not a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
These are the objections I have to the vote. The vote has been increased and is now $6,091,000. In my opinion that vote should go to the trained men of this force and should not be used to pay the guards of public buildings. I believe such guards should be taken on by the public works department, who have the responsibility of erecting the buildings, or that the guarding of these buildings should be the obligation of the departments concerned. The national defence department -takes the responsibility

War Appropriation-Justice
of guarding its own property. I believe that the other public buildings of the government should be guarded by the departments concerned, thus freeing the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to do the work which they have done, without question, with the highest possible regard for the security of the state. With respect to their activities concerned with the apprehension of suspected enemy agents, no suspect receives the benefit of the doubt more freely given than by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. No force takes the trouble, the painstaking trouble, to establish beyond any peradventure of doubt the guilt of the individual who is apprehended. I have very little sympathy with anybody who will say, certainly in the part of the country which I know best, that a man who has been apprehended by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has not received a fair chance.
There is one thing more I want to say about the police. The recent case relative to the registrar in military district No. 2, Toronto, indicates that the force acted with absolute fearlessness, without any suggestion of political pressure, when three of the highest officials in a department of government were apprehended and charged.
I ask the Minister of Justice to promote three objectives in this connection: first, that the force shall continue to be the highly skilled and highly technical body that it has been; second, that the pay of the force should be placed on a level comparable with that of the federal bureau of investigation; third, that the job of being custodians of real estate should be taken away from this great force.

I join with the hon. member who has just spoken in commendation of the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I have had some experience of the work they have done in my own city of Prince Albert, where one of the oldest detachments in western Canada is located. To-day the mounted police need no defender anywhere in this dominion for the magnificent work they have done, particularly during the period of the war. In that connection I wish to mention the work done in the sphere of scientific investigation. In Saskatchewan we have located a scientific laboratory under Doctor Powers. The work which has been done by that department is of so remarkable a nature that it has won the approval not only of the people of my province, but of people outside Canada.
I rise, however, to ask a question of the minister. In view of the fact that to-day the Royal Canadian Mounted Police operates 72537-330}	I
generally throughout the dominion, and that in order to operate successfully, it must cooperate with provincial police forces and also with city and municipal police forces, I suggest, in the interests of a better administration of justice, that some body be set up in this country to operate as a coordinating unit between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the other police bodies. What I have in mind is a body similar in nature to Scotland Yard in Great Britain and the federal bureau of investigation in the United States of America. If such a coordinating corps were set up, the work that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the various police forces throughout the dominion could do would be immeasurably improved. The question I wish to ask the minister is whether consideration is being given to the setting up of such a coordinating body.
Mr. ROSS (Souris); I endorse all the remarks made by the hon. member for York West about this splendid force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. There are a couple of questions I wish to ask the minister before he makes his statement. One is with regard to the cost of living bonus. It is granted to many dominion civil servants, and in view of the work which the members of this great force are doing, and the effect of the increased cost of living especially as regards married members of this force, I hope the government will see its way clear to grant the mounted police a cost of living bonus.
Another question: Is a member of this force who has given splendid service over a period of twenty years or more not entitled either to promotion or to some form of special recognition? It seems to me that when a member has had at least twenty years of service and has a clear record, the department should recognize that service, either by promotion or by some recognition whereby his pay would be improved with corresponding benefit upon his retirement. I trust the minister will make a statement regarding these two points.

Only a member of parliament who has had some connection with the police commission of a municipality can understand these estimates or the functions which this particular department has carried on for so many years so ably and faithfully.
The details of the estimates for the last fiscal year as compared with those for the year 1943-44 indicate careless methods in preparing the war appropriation bill. For example, for the last fiscal year the Minister of Finance in
War Appropriation-Justice

his budget speech gave the estimates for the mounted police for the fiscal year just closed as $4,147,000, but in the details of that I find that the expenditure was only $3,869,507. I would suggest to the head of the department that there should be some other system-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If the hon, member will allow me, the estimate made by the Minister of Finance was quite correct, but it covered all the expenses estimated to March 31. On the mimeographed sheet that I have distributed appear only the accounts that were actually paid before March 31, and the difference will appear in the supplementary estimates that will be tabled within the next few days. The amount mentioned by the Minister of Finance became due but was not paid before March 31. We had the appropriation to pay it, but we had not received the accounts, and the payments were not actually made. So that the amounts unexpended lapsed, and had to be included in the supplementary * estimates for 1943-44, though the amounts are .attributable to accounts which would have been paid in 1942-43 if they had been available.

If the minister had waited until I had completed my statement, I would have said nearly all that he has said. Here are the draft estimates for the last fiscal year, and not one of the items corresponds with the amount actually spent. I am not blaming the head of the department for it; he is one of the most competent men in the public service. My point is that we have had the war appropriation bill before us almost since the beginning of this session. If you go through the various items, you will see that the amounts are sometimes varied on account of the transfer of some items, on account of work not done, on account of a smaller number of people employed, and for various other reasons. They are not really estimates at all. You were prominent in municipal work, Mr. Chairman; I am sure you will agree that in a municipality the estimates almost always check with the actual expenditures.
I realize that the work of the mounted police has gone up by leaps and bounds during the war. Before the war the conditions of work were not very satisfactory to the rank and file of the men, or even to the heads of the department. The commissioner, the bead-quarters staff and all the others worked for very small salaries for many years. The men in the department suffered as a result of the small pay and poor working conditions, and the work done between the two wars was somewhat hampered by the lack of funds. As

I look over the details of these estimates, I find that there were only three small deficits, while on the other hand there were several large unexpended balances, which it is said were caused by the force not being recruited up to establishment, and by the anticipated general organization of the security service being found not necessary. Then I see this statement:
A realignment of allotments, in order to better control expenditures, was made in the fiscal vear 1943-1944 from that submitted for 1942-43. This consisted in 1943-44 in transferring allowances (in lieu of quarters, rations, fuel and light) from "pay and allowances 'to allowances including billeting, messing and provisions .
If we take all the items together, the expenditure for the coming fiscal year is estimated at $6,091,319.40, the exact figures given by the Minister of Finance last March.
There is one other, thing I wish to point out in connection with the mounted police. The war has placed tremendous responsibilities and burdens on the civilian police, the mounted police, the home guard and others right across Canada from coast to coast. For the last six or seven years I have urged that the municipalities should be given some recompense for the federal work that is done by the police departments of the cities' of Toronto, Hamilton and other places throughout the country. There has been the utmost cooperation between the civilian police and the mounted police. I heard the late Colonel Denison, who helped found this great institution, pay tribute on many occasions to the cooperation that has been given by the mounted police to the civilian services of police throughout all these years. I believe the time has come when the federal authority should recognize the work these municipal police departments are doing in connection with the administration of federal laws. It is the function and duty of the provincial attorneys-general to enforce all federal law. As you know, Mr. Chairman, the provincial Rttorneys-general have not the proper staff to do all this and enforce all federal laws, so that they just pass the responsibility over to the municipal police. With the tremendous number of acts, regulations and orders in council being passed by this government, I believe the police of the larger cities are entitled to some recognition of the services they are rendering in this regard. In Australia for many years the federal authorities gave subventions to the cities in connection with the enforcement of the federal laws and aided financially this important work. That was done also in New Zealand, and in many of the states of the United States cities and

War Appropriation-Justice
towns were paid subventions for police services in connection with the enforcement of the federal laws of that country.
When you compare the number of men on the civilian police forces with the number they had a few years ago, and take into consideration the tremendous responsibility that is placed upon the civilian police by the federal powers in war to-day, you can understand that in many cases the local police have not sufficient time to attend to their own most important functions and duties and protect the lives and property of the citizens who pay them, with the result that the burden on the taxpayer has become almost intolerable. I do not see why this government could not compensate the police departments of the municipalities for the war-time federal work they are doing. The mounted police come to the city police and want somebody arrested, or want to take out a warrant or lay an information. The local police have to cooperate with them; a court session is held; witnesses are called; police officers are taken off their beats to give evidence, and the municipality is charged with the entire cost, and the upkeep of those convicted. The whole system is wrong. They do not have that system in the old country, and we should not have it here. The government that passes all these orders and regulations should pay for the work required to enforce them. Other cities such as Hamilton, London, Winnipeg and Vancouver have done this federal work free and have had this matter under consideration; the police chiefs' association have urged that some measure of justice should be given the municipalities along the lines I have indicated.
I believe the mounted police now are getting a very fine type of recruit, and I hope that in future the men will have better working conditions and better pay, after carrying on for many years with very small incomes. Better schedules of pay are urgent. I have been acquainted with the work of the mounted police since shortly after the South African war; I have followed their work in Toronto, not only as a police commissioner but as one who has taken a great interest in the mounted police system, and I can tell you that with their small salaries very few of them have been able to make any provision for their old age. The present minister is to be commended for some improvements he has made in the lot of the men of the department, and I hope he may continue to improve in the future the condition of these men and of all ranks in this fine system of the public service. I urge upon him that this
matter should be taken up with the Minister of Finance, and with the municipalities, which are bearing the brunt of this work. I see the hon. member for Parry Sound in his seat to-night, and realize that he knows a great deal about the administration of justice in the courts, and the work done by the civilian police in aid of federal power. I believe the time has come when the federal power should pay for the services rendered, and the out-ofpocket expenses, along the lines I have indicated.

I desire to join with hon. members who have indicated to the Minister of Justice the worthiness of this course and the fact that the mounted police are underpaid. I know a good deal about their requirements. Before one can join the mounted police force he must have a high type of education. The courses they must undertake are severe. They have to study criminal law; they have to learn how to handle horses; they have to be expert drivers of motor cars; they have to understand ballistics; they have to do laboratory work, and be able to analyse blood stains. This is a course requiring men of a high grade of intelligence.
I believe it was two years ago that hon. members, appreciating the underpayment of the force, expressed themselves strongly, and I believe as a result of their efforts there was a slight increase in pay. If the practice has not been changed-and the minister will know; I am not quite sure-a man who enlists as a, constable must serve for seven long years before he can have a raise in pay of a single dollar or a single ten-cent piece. That ought to be changed.
To my mind, the force is terrifically underpaid. That is not the fault of our Minister of Justice, because he has no authority over their payment. It is a matter which must be dealt with by parliament, or on the minister's recommendation. I know he and his predecessor have had to fight the treasury board. They have been loath to make increases.
Who are "they"?

Well, they are a mysterious entity, of very worthy gentlemen. When we advocate a worthy cause, a worthy application for an increase, one concerning which practically all members of the house are unanimous, and we find we get no results, then in my limited experience I sometimes cast a suspicious eye on the treasury board. I make an appeal here and now to that board, through the minister. It would be but common justice to increase that portion of his estimate which.
War Appropriation-Justice

comes under the heading "pay" by 25 per cent. Even then it could be suggested that the mounted police are underpaid.
They carry out a terrific number of tasks in peace time and also in war time. They have to see about the enforcement of the Customs Act, the Opium and Narcotic Drugs Act, the alcohol legislation, in which they run down stills, and illegal manufacturing of alcohol. They must check the white slave traffic. Those are items which come under their jurisdiction in peace time. But when we add to that the fact that part of the force is the secret service of Canada, corresponding to that magnificent force known as Scotland Yard in the mother country and the federal bureau of investigation under J. Edgar Hoover in Washington, then we realize that in war time their task becomes stupendous.
They have to search every outgoing and incoming vessel in every harbour on both the Pacific, and the Atlantic coasts. When we remember the millions of tons of shipping we have sent successfully across the Atlantic ocean, and the fact that these men, in all kinds of weather, have to make sure that no damage will come to those vessels, and with that in mind have to enter the holds and perioral the most difficult tasks to see that no sabotage is being committed, we realize that they carry on a wonderful piece of work.
There is a condemnation, as I see it, in the very memorandum furnished to us. It is a condemnation, not of the minister, but of us, as a parliament; because under item 3' we find this:
The large unexpended balances under allotments of "pay" and "security service" were caused by (a) not being recruited up to establishment.
The reason why they are not recruited up to establishment is that we cannot get the type of young men in Canada who are required for this work to enter the force, on account of the pittance we pay them. And in war time, and at all times, it is incumbent upon this country to see that the force is properly paid.
I would just remind the committee of one factor. Many of these men are married. There is a restriction about marriage without the consent of the authorities. I should like to pay great tribute to General Stuart Wood, the efficient head of this force. The committee will remember that he was selected by us to escort their majesties, and he took charge of their welfare on the trip they made across Canada and into the United States just before the war. He is a magnificent officer, and the same might be said of his inspectors,

the higher command, and right down through the line to the last constable. They are a splendid force.
When the married mounted police officer leaves home in the morning, bidding his wife and perhaps his children good-bye, those people at home do not know whether or not he will come back at night. He must perform services in contact with and in suppression of the most dangerous type of criminal any country can produce. He takes his life in his hands every day he dons his uniform and goes on duty.
Therefore I appeal to the minister, and to the treasury board behind him, to add twenty-five per cent to the pay of these men, adjusting it with reason, throughout the entire payroll of this magnificent force.

I should like to associate myself in a most emphatic manner with the remarks of the hon. member for Parry Sound. All he has said is entirely correct. I
believe we could go even further than twenty-five per cent, and still leave a most magnificent and deserving force very much underpaid.

I should like to
speak from the experience I have had with the mounted police in Toronto. I believe I could not voice sufficient appreciation of the work they have done, and the efficency of the lorce in that city. They have great difficulties to contend with, one of which is that they must deal with other police forces, and in those dealings must be at all times diplomatic. Then, they must not go outside the bounds of provincial rights.
I would express my appreciation of the force, from the commissioner down to the constables, and would make special mention of those men who are engaged in secret investigations of one kind or another. They are doing a magnificent job for Canada, although it has very little glory connected with it. Many of these men do not wear uniforms. I believe the only way in which their services can be properly appreciated is by increasing their pay. I agree with the hon. member for Parry Sound, the hon. member for Souris and others who have spoken, that the cost-of-living bonus certainly should be given to the men on this force. Their pay is very small, when one considers the work they do.
Another point is that in Canada this force is the symbol of law and order. The sight of our red-coated mounted police around the government buildings in various Canadian cities is an incentive to law and order. Seeing

War Appropriation-Justice
these men. and having a knowledge of the history of the force helps to make law-abiding citizens. Their duties call them all over the country, as far north almost to the north pole; sometimes they have to go out of the country, to Australia or some place like that. As the hon. member for Parry Sound said, those men who are engaged on secret investigations do not know whether they are going to come back. They are always in danger. While the force has a certain attraction for young men, I think the pay and allowances are not sufficient to make young men want to make this their life work. I agree with the hon. member for Parry Sound when he says that a considerable increase in pay should be given these men. The cost of living has gone up some seventeen per cent, and it would not be out of the way to have the mounted police receive a substantial increase. I wish to congratulate the commissioner and the assistant commissioner-I know of some of the work he has done-for having kept up the high standards of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to identify the Progressive Conservative party with the suggestions which have been made for better financial treatment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I am not going into this matter to-night at any length, because earlier in the session I raised this question. I should like to suggest to the minister that the pay and allowances of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should be reviewed at once with the object of bringing them up to the standard of service they are rendering Canada in this wartime period.
Mr. GILLI'S: There is some information I should like to get in connection with this item. At the latter part of last session the minister brought down a special appropriation to set up what I understood was a security police force. I assume that that would be included in these war appropriations now before us. Before I go into that matter, I should like to take a moment or two to reply to some of the things the hon. member for Parry Sound had to say about me a few moments ago.
That does not come under the police force item.

Nor did the remarks he made a few minutes ago. It has never been my custom to delay the committee, because I generally try to be as relevant as possible to the item under consideration. On two occasions during this session the hon. member for Parry Sound has deliberately gone out of his
way to make a personal attack upon myself without having any evidence to support it. As a noted criminal lawyer he seems to have little respect for the laws of debate in this house. I have deliberately avoided getting into the discussion, because I try to observe the rules of this house.
As I said a moment ago, on two occasions the hon. member for Parry Sound has been permitted to rise in his place in this house and make an attack upon me without any evidence to support it except about four lines that were taken out of the context of a forty-minute speech of mine by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and placed on the record. That is the evidence upon which the hon. member for Parry Sound based his remarks to-night and on a previous occasion. At that time I told him that when the opportunity presented itself under an appropriate item I intended to reply to the hon. member for York-Sunbury. Neither of the hon. members is in the chamber at the moment.
We know why the hon. member for Parry Sound made the remarks he did this evening. It is obvious that he did so for political reasons. If he were as patriotic as he would have us believe, he would not have started a discussion and taken up the time of the committee in order to make the remarks he did. His attempt to-night to discredit the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and myself in particular was based upon four lines from a speech of mine which were placed on the record by the hon. member for York-Sunbury on March 18, 1943, when he quoted the Hamilton Spectator. I did not reply at that time because I would not have been in order, nor did I reply to the hon. member for Parry Sound when he interjected a similar tirade against me. I did not want to take up the time of the house. But when the same matter is raised three times during the same session I think it is up to me to defend myself.
The basis of the statement by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, which in turn was the basis of the statement by the hon. member for Parry Sound-he had no knowledge of it; he had no idea of what had been said; yet he stood up and tried to mislead the people of this country into believing that a certain thing had happened at a certain time-was a report of a meeting which I had attended in Hamilton. I was invited to this meeting by members of a reputable organization who are just as interested in and perhaps making a greater contribution to the war effort than the hon. member for Parry Sound. I discussed the subject they gave me to discuss, and I made a forty-minute speech,
War Appropriation-Justice

During that speech I was asked whether I thought the full aims and objects for which the people of Britain were fighting the war would be attained under the present British government. I have my own opinion as to the aims and objectives for which the British people are fighting that war and, exercising that opinion and the right to express it, regardless of what the Hamilton Spectator had to say, I said that in my opinion when the British army was brought back from Dunkirk, battered, practically disarmed, having been caught in a trap which, in my view, had been prepared by the ruling classes of France not only for the British but for the French army, it was the ordinary, common citizen who had rescued his army. That is a statement of fact. I said that I thought the British people were waging a war against the leadership which had placed their army in that position at Dunkirk, and that when this war is over, leadership from the classes in Britain who were making the major portion of the sacrifices would be selected to bring about those changes which I visualize the British people as fighting for and a system which will preclude the possibility of a repetition of a world war in the next generation.
With respect to Churchill, I said that I in no way detracted from his ability as a war leader, but that in my opinion the British people were not fighting for British imperialism in the aftermath of this war, and that when the war was off their hands they would in their own way decide who should write the peace and in what kind of society they would live. Fighting the war and rearranging a country's economy are two entirely different jobs and require men of different calibre. That was my answer. I detracted in no way from Churchill's ability as a great leader in the crisis of war, but I do not now nor did I in the past visualize the restoration of the status quo.
Many hon. members have attended meetings, but they do not assume any responsibility for what some pin-headed reporter may write in his paper. As to this reporter for the Hamilton Spectator, I never saw him, and did not know he was there, and yet the hon. member for York-Sunbury takes as his authority what was written in some obscure paper by somebody over whom I had no control and no responsibility for whatever, and puts that on the records of this house as gospel.
If the hon. member's remarks were not correctly reported, why did he not write to the paper and correct them? Why wait until now to do so?

My answer to that is this. There are 625 newspapers circulating in this province and I do not know how many there are altogether in Canada. If you have time to read all the newspapers in Canada and answer all the stuff you see in them about your party, you are not going to do much work in this house. I had never seen the article in the Hamilton Spectator; I have not seen it yet; I never knew anything about it until the hon. member for York-Sunbury put it on the records of this house, and then I went to the library and looked for it, but someone had it and I have not seen it yet.
The hon. member for Parry Sound has endeavoured on two occasions to belittle the members of this group so far as the war effort is concerned. I am not holding any other member of his party responsible for his utterances, but speaking for myself I say that I will put my record at any time on this Hansard or in any journal in this country alongside the record of the hon. member for Parry Sound as a citizen of this country. When it comes to serving this country on the basis of patriotism and being willing to do something for our institutions and their maintenance I will put my record at any time alongside that of the hon. member for Parry Sound.
You should have heard your friends in that group before you joined them.
I am not talking about that. I am talking of the attack that was made on me personally in the house, and it has been done three times.
You are judged by the company you keep.
The company can take care of itself.

I think I have the floor, Mr. Chairman. I am answering the hon. member for Parry Sound. I hold him responsible for his utterances. I have already demonstrated my desire and willingness to do something for this country in any way that I can and I still have the same feeling I had when I was serving as a young man in the last war. It is all right when you are a grandfather and cannot go yourself to sit back and belittle other .people. It is easy to be brave then and urge somebody else to go. I spent my seventeenth birthday in the front line in France fighting for this country, and if I had not been elected as a member of parliament in 1940 I would have been there to-day.

They probably would not take you.

War Appropriation-Justice

Yes, they would. I would have got over there in some way. I say that such talk ill-becomes a man of the standing of the hon. member for Parry Sound, and if he has not anything more to contribute to this house than that kind of cheap political trickery which has nothing at all to do with the matter under discussion-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The word
"trickery" is unparliamentary, and I would ask the hon. member to withdraw it.

If it is unparliamentary, I will withdraw it, Mr. Chairman, but I still think it is rather cheap to rise in the house and precipitate a discussion and bring out that kind of stuff when everyone in the house is trying to conclude its business. I have sat here three times and taken this talk that was entirely uncalled for, and I rise to-night to correct the impression which the hon. member for Parry Sound persists in trying to create. He tries to play up something that has absolutely no basis in fact; does it for nothing but political advantage, and takes the hon. member for York-Sunbury for his authority. I can take any speech made in this house, and if I wanted to pull a sentence out of its context I could read it into the record and make it appear that the hon. member had said exactly the reverse of what he did. It ill-behooves any member of this house in this time of war to go back fifteen years in the history of Canada and discuss matters on the basis of militarism. I could take the record of all three parties; I could take the Prime Minister's statements in 1937 and just prior to the outbreak of war in 1939 and put on the records the opinions that were held at that time. But conditions change, and it is a wise man who changes his mind once in a while. The fool goes on forever in the one direction. I do not find fault with people for changing their minds on the basis of changed conditions. A country that is flexible enough to change its attitude to suit the growth of new conditions is a healthy country. The only bind of people you find fixed and immovable are those like those you find in Europe who are regimented and have a gun held at their heads to make them toe the line.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that I had to take up this amount of time, but I am not responsible. I intended to let the whole thing go. But it has been done before, and I felt that the time had arrived for me to aay something about it.
The question I rose to ask was this. Toward the end of the last session there was a large appropriation before the house for the purpose
of setting up in Canada a body of security police, and the Minister of Justice stated at that time that their pay and allowances would be in conformity with the pay and allowances of the armed forces. This police force was not to be uniformed, and someone was to be brought from the old country to organize it. I should like to know what amount of this appropriation is allocated to that branch of the service.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The security service that was then contemplated was not organized on the original scale. The matter was reconsidered, and it is for that reason that there was allocated out of the war appropriation of last year $1,154,800, of which only $132,682.62 was expended, and for the service on the scale that has been organized and performed in a satisfactory way the amount required this year is $200,000.
There were four or five other questions asked by some hon. members to which I should like to reply, but before doing so I wish to express my own gratification, as the minister responsible for the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to all hon. members who have spoken and who have paid such a high and well-deserved tribute to the faithful and efficient performance of their duties by the members of this force.

Pass that on to the treasury board.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The treasury board, of which I am a member and whose meetings I attended when the matter was considered, did to some degree acquiesce in or consent to the requests I submitted, and since the voting of the supplementary estimates at the beginning of this session an increase has been made in the allowances to those veteran guards who are paid out of this war appropriation. There has been some confusion here. These are not estimates required for pay and allowances of regular members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. With respect to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police there has been since 1941 an increase in pay and allowances of 30 per cent for the ordinary constables. They were receiving $3.85 a day and are receiving $5 a day. I am not saying that is a sufficient compensation for the valuable services they perform, but one difficulty that has had to be contended with is the ceiling that has been placed on all wages and allowances, and that has been stated as an insuperable difficulty in making any more substantial increases in these allowances. That takes care of the suggestion made by two hon. members, that these
War Appropriation-Justice

members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should receive a cost of living bonus. Instead of receiving a cost of living bonus, there was an increase in the allowances of from $1.60 to $2.25 for the ordinary constables. No increase was made in the allowances of the members of the force who were already receiving as much as $2.25 a day. The superior officers of the force agreed to stay at the rates of their own allowances, provided the ordinary constables were brought to $2.25 a day.
The member for York West has suggested that they are performing work equal to that performed in the United States by the federal bureau of investigation. I fully agree. I believe that all Canadians are proud of the fact that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is quite as efficient as any similar organization in any other country. However, it must be admitted that throughout the whole of our public service in Canada, for work being performed just as efficiently by Canadians as similar work is performed elsewhere by citizens of other countries, the compensation is not as large.

Has the question been
considered whether the departments concerned should perform this task of guarding their buildings? The railways guard their own property and so do the defence departments. Has any consideration been given to that question?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not recently. Prior to 1920 there was a dominion police force that performed the service of guarding public buildings. At that time it was thought desirable to amalgamate the two services and place them under the control of the commissioner, and the matter has not been reconsidered since. That is the historical explanation of the fact that members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are now performing duties that do not appear to us to be of the importance of the duties with which they are usually connected in the public mind.
The hon. member pointed to a recent prosecution which has been instituted in Toronto as evidence that no political pressure has any effect on these servants of the public, and I am glad to have that recognition. I hope it will be possible always to have the same recognition. There should never be any political pressure affecting in any way the performance of the duties which devolve upon this force.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Or any governmental
department.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Or any governmental department; but when it comes to the administration of justice that is a matter with which I am especially concerned and with respect

Questions
to which I am particularly cautious that there shall not be even a ground for any suspicion of political intervention.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I suggest that the minister spread his caution over the whole governmental field.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The administration of justice takes in a pretty broad field. I hope it will be possible for hon. members to give the same tribute to the other branches connected with the administration of justice. That is something which, like Caesar's wife, must be above all suspicion.
The question was raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre as to the desirability of there being some agency to coordinate the work of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the provincial police and the municipal police. The commissioner, whose experience is quite extensive, informs me that in fact there is more coordination between the various police services in Canada than there is in the United States, and that he is satisfied that the coordination here compares not unfavourably with that between the police forces of the United Kingdom. There is always room for improvement, and the hon. member may be sure that this is a matter which is very close to the heart of the commissioner and receives attentive consideration from him.
The statement of the hon. member for Parry Sound that it is seven years before a man joining the Royal Canadian Mounted Police can obtain any promotion or increase of compensation is not quite accurate. There is an increase in compensation with each year of service, but it requires seven years from the time of enlistment before one becomes a full constable with the maximum pay of the full constable.

What is the maximum pay of a full constable?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The maximum pay and allowances of a full constable is $5 a day.

There is one question with respect to coordination that I should like to ask the minister. I was reading the other day that the assistant commissioner, speaking before the Police Chiefs' Association of Canada, pointed out that there was a need of some coordinating body such as I suggested.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes; but there is improvement and, I think, from the ground up. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police has established a school which is open to all officers of police forces, whether municipal, provincial or federal, and there are members
of municipal and provincial forces attending that school.
There will be other opportunities for discussion, when the civil estimates of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are under consideration, and I feel that perhaps it would not be the temper of the committee to delay this further. If there are matters which I have unintentionally overlooked in my haste to give as many answers as possible, I would be glad to supply them when the civil estimates are under consideration, at some other sitting.

Progress reported.
